Alcohol Use Disorder

Psychiatric MONDO:0007079 Pathograph 67 Show in embeddings browser Substance Use Disorder Mental Health Disorder

Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a heterogeneous pattern of alcohol use causing clinically significant impairment or distress. DSM-5-TR diagnosis requires at least two of eleven criteria within a year and grades severity by criterion count; tolerance and withdrawal are possible criteria rather than requirements. Genetic liability, environment, reinforcement, learning and exposure-related adaptations contribute probabilistically. The three-stage addiction framework organizes relevant mechanisms but is not a necessary linear course for every patient. Remission, recurrence and sustained recovery all occur.

Inheritance

1
Polygenic (multifactorial) liability HP:0010982
Liability is polygenic and depends on environmental exposure. Protective ADH1B and ALDH2 alleles affect ethanol metabolism; their effects do not make this a Mendelian disorder. Twin and adoption meta-analysis estimates roughly 50% heritability in the studied populations, with a modest shared-environment component. Heritability is a population variance estimate, not the fraction of an individual case caused by genes.
polygenic inheritance
Show evidence (3 references)
PMID:25171596 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"AUD is approximately 50% heritable."
Meta-analysis of 12 twin and 5 adoption studies gives the reference heritability estimate for AUD liability.
PMID:25171596 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"We also found evidence for modest shared environmental effects suggesting that environmental factors also contribute to the familial aggregation of AUDs."
Supports the multifactorial framing: familial aggregation is not purely genetic.
PMID:38062264 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"We observed a high degree of cross-ancestral similarity in the genetic architecture of PAU and identified 110 independent risk variants in within- and cross-ancestry analyses."
The largest multi-ancestry GWAS of problematic alcohol use demonstrates the highly polygenic architecture expected under multifactorial inheritance.

Discussions and Knowledge Gaps

3
Which experimental receptor and stress-system adaptations causally contribute to clinically defined AUD in humans?
HUMAN MODEL MISMATCH aud_model_translation
Attached to
pathophysiology#GABA-A Receptor Redistribution pathophysiology#CRF-Associated Stress Signaling pathophysiology#Dynorphin–Kappa-Opioid Signaling pathophysiology#TLR4-Dependent Inflammatory Signaling
Rodent exposure, preference and drinking-in-the-dark paradigms interrogate distinct endpoints. They do not reproduce every diagnostic feature, and region-, time- and genotype-dependent effects limit a universal mechanistic chain. Human imaging, genetic associations and treatment efficacy cannot by themselves prove mediation through these specific experimental processes.

Cross-sectional psychiatric associations and MRI differences do not isolate causal direction. The depression study selected people with major depressive disorder, not an unselected AUD population. Genetic PAU combines heterogeneous diagnoses and questionnaire measures; current polygenic scores are not sufficient for individual clinical risk prediction.

Pathophysiology

29
Polygenic Liability
Common-variant associations contribute to liability rather than determining disease. The 2023 meta-analysis combines 165,952 AUD or dependence cases, controls and AUDIT problems scores in 1,079,947 participants; it is not a cohort of one million diagnosed cases. The 110 variants are the union of within- and cross-ancestry results, and most data are European ancestry. Specific nonmetabolic variant-to-neural causal routes remain unresolved.
Downstream
Impaired Control over Alcohol Use Association establishes probabilistic liability; the intervening molecular and behavioral mechanisms are incompletely resolved.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:38062264 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"In total, 110 unique variants were associated with PAU in either the within-ancestry or cross-ancestry analyses (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Table 1)."
The union of within- and cross-ancestry signals supports distributed susceptibility; it does not identify a single necessary mechanism of impaired control.
PMID:38062264 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human Clinical
"Despite the high genetic correlation between AUD and AUDIT–P, they are not identical traits, which introduces heterogeneity."
The authors explicitly distinguish diagnosed AUD from AUDIT-P, limiting disease-specific interpretation of the combined PAU analysis.
Repeated Ethanol Exposure
Repeated alcohol intake supplies the exposure for intoxication, neuroadaptation and medical complications. Dose, timing, host susceptibility and environment influence outcomes; exposure alone does not establish AUD. This exposure node is separate from enzymatic metabolism and from the impaired-control phenotype.
Animal models
Alcohol-preferring P rats Rattus norvegicus measures Voluntary intake and binge-access endpoints model high alcohol exposure.
High-alcohol-drinking HAD rat lines Rattus norvegicus measures Selected high-drinking lines model voluntary exposure.
HAP/LAP preference QTL mouse cross Mus musculus measures Alcohol preference varied in a segregating HAP1 × LAP1 F2 cross and was linked to a chromosome 9 QTL; no single increase relative to a control is asserted.
HDID selected-line aversion and reward assays Mus musculus measures Blood ethanol concentrations after a four-hour drinking-in-the-dark test increased in both selected replicate lines relative to the founding generation; aversion and reward were assessed in separate experiments.
Downstream
Acute GABA-A Signaling Modulation Ethanol acutely modulates inhibitory GABA-A signaling in neuronal preparations. This pharmacological effect is distinct from chronic receptor redistribution and does not imply identical effects at every receptor subtype.
Acute NMDA Receptor Inhibition Ethanol inhibits NMDA-receptor-mediated calcium influx in the reviewed neuronal experiments; the acute receptor action is separate from chronic glutamate adaptation.
Alcohol-Evoked Endogenous Opioid Signaling Drinking produces an opioid-sensitive PET ligand-displacement response in human accumbens and orbitofrontal cortex; the intervening release machinery is not resolved by this experiment.
Mesolimbic Dopamine Reinforcement Alcohol engages mesolimbic reinforcement circuitry through several neuronal and receptor routes; the dopamine synthesis does not establish one exclusive upstream relay.
GABA-A Receptor Redistribution Single and repeated ethanol regimens alter receptor trafficking and surface composition in rodents. The exact signaling route and persistence depend on the regimen and neuronal compartment.
Altered Glutamate Homeostasis Exposure and withdrawal are associated with altered glutamate regulation. Human regional measurements and repeated-vapor rodent experiments do not imply a single uniform trajectory.
CRF-Associated Stress Signaling The withdrawal framework recruits extended-amygdala CRF systems after repeated drug exposure; complete mediation of the human stress response remains unresolved.
Dynorphin–Kappa-Opioid Signaling Dependent-animal and neurocircuitry evidence implicates dynorphin signaling in withdrawal-related stress, without establishing its recruitment as universal in AUD.
Withdrawal-Associated Reward Deficit Withdrawal from chronic exposure lowers dopamine activity in reviewed rodent experiments; the transition to a human subjective reward deficit requires additional interpretation.
Habitual Alcohol Seeking Repeated seeking and reinforcement permit habitual control to develop in the rat paradigm; the predictor relationship does not prove that exposure alone determines later compulsivity.
Thiamine Deficiency Heavy drinking can reduce nutritional intake and impair thiamine availability. These known nutritional intermediates are not expanded into separate nodes here.
TLR4-Dependent Inflammatory Signaling Chronic ethanol exposure produces TLR4-dependent inflammatory responses in mouse and astrocyte models; the experiments do not establish ethanol as a direct TLR4 ligand.
Alcohol Cue Responsivity Repeated pairing and learning offer an interpretation of cue-associated responses; the imaging synthesis alone does not prove longitudinal sensitization.
Impaired Executive Control The framework describes an exposure-associated contribution to executive dysfunction; pre-existing liability and other factors cannot be excluded by cross-sectional imaging.
Withdrawal-Associated Autonomic Activation Withdrawal after sustained heavy exposure can activate autonomic responses in physiologically dependent individuals.
Hepatic Steatosis Alcohol metabolism and disturbed lipid handling connect sustained exposure to hepatic fat accumulation; those known liver-specific intermediates are curated in Alcoholic_Liver_Disease.
Cirrhosis Alcohol-associated liver disease can progress from steatosis through hepatitis to cirrhosis in a subset of patients; the liver-specific intermediate processes are not expanded in this AUD graph.
Dilated Cardiomyopathy Chronic alcohol toxicity can produce myocardial injury and adverse remodeling before ventricular dilation; the organ-specific intermediates are not expanded here.
Pancreatitis Alcohol-related pancreatic injury and inflammation can lead to acute or chronic pancreatitis through organ-specific pathways omitted from this graph.
Peripheral Neuropathy Direct neurotoxicity and nutritional injury are recognized routes from chronic alcohol use to peripheral neuropathy; the nerve-specific intermediates are not expanded here.
Acetaldehyde Accumulation Ethanol is converted by ADH enzymes to acetaldehyde; accumulation depends on the balance between this known formation step and ALDH-mediated clearance.

url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK436003/ SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Human Clinical
"The fact that not every person who drinks alcohol will necessarily experience a loss of control and progression to addiction indicates that AUD is not solely driven by exposure to alcohol."
The clinical synthesis distinguishes alcohol exposure from the additional susceptibility required for impaired control and addiction.
Increased ADH1B-Mediated Ethanol Oxidation
In carriers of protective high-activity ADH1B alleles, faster enzyme-catalyzed conversion of ethanol to acetaldehyde is proposed to contribute to aversive effects and reduced dependence risk. Purified-enzyme kinetics do not imply the same fold change in whole-body clearance or a universal flushing response.

PMID:17718394 SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS In Vitro
"certain ADH1B and ADH1C alleles encode particularly active ADH enzymes, resulting in more rapid conversion of alcohol (i.e., ethanol) to acetaldehyde"

Reduced ALDH2-Mediated Acetaldehyde Clearance
The ALDH2*2 variant markedly reduces conversion of acetaldehyde to acetate. Under alcohol exposure this favors acetaldehyde accumulation; the allele is protective against dependence rather than a monogenic cause of AUD.

Acetaldehyde Accumulation
Reduced clearance, or an imbalance between formation and clearance, increases exposure to the toxic ethanol metabolite acetaldehyde. This conditional metabolic branch is especially well supported for reduced ALDH2 activity.
Downstream
Acetaldehyde-Associated Aversion Acetaldehyde accumulation elicits downstream vasoactive and autonomic responses that contribute to aversion; these physiological intermediates are not expanded in this graph.
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:17718394 SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS In Vitro
"A variant of the ALDH2 gene encodes an essentially inactive ALDH enzyme, resulting in acetaldehyde accumulation"
Reduced ALDH2 function decreases aldehyde clearance and favors acetaldehyde accumulation during drinking; its association with lower dependence risk is protective.
Acetaldehyde-Associated Aversion
Flushing, nausea and tachycardia after acetaldehyde accumulation can discourage drinking. This is a protective modifier pathway, not an obligatory step in the progression of AUD. Disulfiram deliberately engages an aversive response by inhibiting aldehyde clearance.
Downstream
Facial Flushing After Alcohol Intake Flushing is one component of the exposure-dependent aversive reaction.
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:17718394 SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Human Clinical
"Acetaldehyde is a toxic substance whose accumulation leads to a highly aversive reaction that includes facial flushing, nausea, and rapid heart beat (i.e., tachycardia)."
The review explicitly connects accumulated acetaldehyde with flushing, nausea and tachycardia, supporting an aversive modifier rather than a required AUD pathway.
Acute GABA-A Signaling Modulation
Acute ethanol can enhance GABAergic inhibition through effects that depend on receptor composition, synaptic compartment, dose and brain region. The review evidence includes rodent and cellular work; it does not establish uniform potentiation at every receptor or a single necessary route to human intoxication. GABAergic neurons supply the inhibitory transmitter; receptor-bearing target neurons need not themselves be GABAergic.

Alcohol-Evoked Endogenous Opioid Signaling
Human positron-emission tomography after drinking showed displacement of a mu-opioid radioligand in nucleus accumbens and orbitofrontal cortex, interpreted as endogenous opioid release. Alcohol Cue Responsivity
Alcohol-associated cues evoke brain responses that can correlate with craving. The meta-analysis included 28 studies of heavy-drinking/AUD samples; within-case ventral-striatal activation was not equivalent to a significant case-versus-control difference. Region-of-interest selection, heterogeneous ascertainment and mainly male samples limit generalization. This is an associative circuit finding, not a validated clinical biomarker.

GABA-A Receptor Redistribution
Rodent chronic-intermittent-ethanol studies and cell/slice assays describe time- and compartment-dependent changes in GABA-A receptor surface composition. Reduced tonic ethanol sensitivity can coexist with increased sensitivity of some synaptic currents. Single-dose changes can reverse, while repeated regimens produce longer persistence; endpoint-specific tolerance is not universal receptor loss or proven lifelong human dysfunction. Hippocampal and cortical pyramidal-neuron recordings are among the preparations supporting these changes.

The review distinguishes persistent receptor remodeling after repeated exposure from the reversible single-dose changes; this is a rat result, not a human threshold.
Altered Glutamate Homeostasis
Repeated ethanol exposure and withdrawal can alter glutamate release, uptake and receptor regulation. Elevated extracellular glutamate is supported in particular rodent dependence models, while human spectroscopy results vary by region and timing and do not all show elevation. The whole process should not be reduced to universal NMDA-receptor upregulation.

Withdrawal-Associated CNS Hyperexcitability
Reduction or cessation after sustained heavy exposure in a physiologically dependent person can uncover altered inhibitory/excitatory regulation. This contributes to tremor, insomnia, hallucinations and, in severe cases, seizures or delirium. Withdrawal is neither universal in AUD nor a requirement for diagnosis.
Downstream
Tremor Withdrawal-related neural hyperexcitability can manifest as tremor through motor-system output.
Alcohol Withdrawal Seizures Excessive synchronized neuronal activity can produce a generalized withdrawal seizure in susceptible patients.
Alcohol Withdrawal Delirium Severe withdrawal can impair attention and awareness through distributed brain dysfunction; hyperexcitability is contributory rather than a complete explanation of delirium.
Withdrawal Hallucinations Withdrawal-associated circuit dysfunction can produce hallucinations; the precise sensory-network mediation is incompletely resolved.
Insomnia Withdrawal-related arousal can disrupt sleep through central sleep-wake regulation.
Nausea and Vomiting Withdrawal can produce nausea and vomiting through central and autonomic responses; the cited clinical account does not resolve their exact mediation.
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:25307573 SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Human Clinical
"Clinical features of alcohol withdrawal include signs of central nervous system hyperexcitability, heightened autonomic nervous system activation, and a constellation of symptoms contributing to psychologic discomfort and negative affect."
The human withdrawal syndrome includes both central hyperexcitability and autonomic activation; this clinical description alone does not identify a particular receptor mediator.
Withdrawal-Associated Autonomic Activation
Autonomic activation during withdrawal can produce tachycardia, sweating and elevated blood pressure. This component is separated from cortical excitability because controlling heart rate or blood pressure does not prevent withdrawal seizures or delirium.
Downstream
Withdrawal Tachycardia Sympathetic efferent signaling increases cardiac rate during withdrawal.
Withdrawal Hyperhidrosis Autonomic sudomotor output increases sweating during withdrawal.
Withdrawal Hypertension Autonomic cardiovascular output can raise blood pressure during withdrawal.

url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf SUPPORT DIRECT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Human Clinical
"Clinical signs include sweating, elevated blood pressure, tachycardia, hyperthermia, and hyperactive reflexes."
The guideline explicitly lists sweating, tachycardia and elevated blood pressure among withdrawal signs, supporting the autonomic branch.
CRF-Associated Stress Signaling
The addiction framework implicates CRF signaling in dependence-related stress and negative affect, with much of the causal evidence from rodent regional pharmacology. This is distinct from the nondependent VTA CRF-binding-protein/CRF2 drinking-in-the-dark experiment; that result is not evidence of central-amygdala CRF1 mediation.

Dynorphin–Kappa-Opioid Signaling
Dynorphin and kappa-opioid signaling are implicated in aversion and dependence-related drinking in experimental literature. Effects depend on timing, region, sex and model; knockout findings are not uniform. The conference review contains preliminary reports, and human postmortem expression associations do not prove that blocking this pathway treats AUD.

Withdrawal-Associated Reward Deficit
Reviewed dependence models show reduced dopamine neuronal activity or basal striatal dopamine during withdrawal. These observations support a reward-deficit hypothesis but should not be generalized to every brain region, exposure phase or individual with AUD.

Withdrawal-Associated Negative Affect
Anxiety, dysphoria and other aversive states can motivate renewed drinking for relief. Hyperkatifeia is a cross-drug heuristic framework integrating reward deficits and stress signaling, not a biomarker or a required stage in every patient. Persistent symptoms also require assessment for independent psychiatric illness.
Downstream
Impaired Control over Alcohol Use Relief of aversive withdrawal states can motivate renewed use through negative reinforcement; this does not account for all patterns of impaired control.
Anxiety Anxiety can be part of an aversive withdrawal state, without implying all independent anxiety disorders arise through this route.

PMID:33318153 SUPPORT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Other

The review defines heightened negative affect during withdrawal and proposes its motivational role; it does not establish a single causal neurochemical route.
Habitual Alcohol Seeking
In alcohol-preferring male rats, devaluation-insensitive seeking predicted subsequent punishment-resistant seeking and quinine-resistant drinking. The cited abstract supplies behavioral evidence; its background anatomical account is not a new direct assay of dorsal-striatal dopamine or proof of the same causal sequence in humans.

Downstream
Impaired Control over Alcohol Use In the rat paradigm, stronger habitual control predicted punishment-resistant seeking; extrapolation to human impaired control remains indirect.

PMID:33955649 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Model Organism
"After seeking behaviour was well established, subjects that had developed greater resistance to outcome devaluation (were more habitual) were more likely to show punishment-resistant (compulsive) alcohol seeking."
Outcome-devaluation resistance predicted punishment-resistant seeking in selected rats; the association does not prove that habitual control alone causes human compulsive drinking.
Impaired Executive Control
Reduced inhibitory control and altered decision-making can contribute to difficulty limiting alcohol use in the addiction framework. Cross-sectional MRI differences in AUD provide anatomical associations, not proof that alcohol caused progressive atrophy or that a measured structural difference mediated an executive deficit.

Impaired Control over Alcohol Use
Impaired control and persistent use despite harm are clinical manifestations to which reinforcement, learned cue responses, aversive-state relief and executive-control problems may contribute. These routes can coexist but are not a mandatory ordered sequence, and DSM criteria allow heterogeneous presentations.
Downstream
Addictive Alcohol Use The node describes the impaired-control component of the clinical phenotype, while individual DSM criterion combinations vary.
Problematic Alcohol Consumption Persistent impaired control can produce problematic consumption and related impairment.
Repeated Ethanol Exposure Difficulty limiting use can perpetuate exposure, creating a feedback relationship rather than a necessary one-way progression.

The guideline states the DSM-5-TR clinical threshold, supporting the diagnostic construct rather than a molecular cause of addiction.
Thiamine Deficiency
Poor intake and alcohol-related interference with thiamine handling can produce deficiency and neurologic complications. Nutritional deficiency is an exposure-associated pathway distinct from reinforcement and receptor adaptation; not everyone with AUD develops it.

TLR4-Dependent Inflammatory Signaling
In female mice exposed to ethanol for five months and in neonatal rodent astrocyte preparations, Tlr4 deletion or knockdown attenuated inflammatory responses. Direct ethanol binding to TLR4 was not established. The constitutive whole-body knockout does not isolate an astrocyte- or microglia-autonomous mechanism in vivo or prove this pathway causes human AUD.

Cortical Caspase-3 Activation The mouse comparison associates TLR4 function with ethanol-induced cortical caspase-3 cleavage; the responsible cell type and intervening death pathway remain unresolved.

In neonatal rodent astrocyte cultures, ethanol increased nuclear NF-kappa-B p65 signaling, and TLR4 knockdown or deficiency attenuated it. These cell-culture findings are separate from whole-cortex measurements and do not establish a universal patient biomarker.

GFAP and CD11b immunoreactivity increased in the cortex of ethanol-exposed wild-type mice. VTA CRF2-Associated Drinking Modulation
In male mice, local VTA CRF2 antagonism reduced nondependent drinking-in-the-dark intake; CRF-binding-protein interference added to the effect under tested conditions. The study did not assay dopamine, NMDA currents or physical receptor interactions. CRF-binding-protein blockade was ineffective in central amygdala and in the dependent intermittent-access VTA condition.

Oral Naltrexone
Action: PharmacotherapyNCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment is this clinical intervention This treatment is Pharmacotherapy (NCIT:C15986). NCIT:C15986 is a clinical intervention from the NCI Thesaurus. NCIT:C15986
Agent: naltrexone CHEBI:7465 Chemical Entities of Biological Interest (CHEBI) Relation: this treatment uses this therapeutic agent This treatment uses naltrexone (CHEBI:7465). CHEBI:7465 is a therapeutic agent from Chemical Entities of Biological Interest.
Platform: Small molecule
First-line opioid-receptor antagonist for adults with moderate to severe AUD seeking abstinence or reduced drinking. Oral 50 mg/day has the strongest formulation-specific trial evidence for reducing return to heavy drinking; pair with appropriate psychosocial support and patient-defined goals. Current opioid use and acute hepatitis or liver failure are important contraindications; assess future opioid analgesia needs.
Mechanism Target:
INHIBITS Alcohol-Evoked Endogenous Opioid Signaling — Opioid-receptor antagonism blocks signaling rather than proving that suppression of a particular endogenous peptide or dopamine relay mediates clinical response.

First-line medication for an abstinence goal, generally started after withdrawal and abstinence. Trial evidence supports reduced return to any drinking, without a clear benefit for preventing return to heavy drinking. Severe renal impairment is a contraindication and moderate impairment requires dose adjustment.

Give thiamine promptly to prevent or treat deficiency-related neurologic injury. ASAM favors parenteral administration for poor nutrition, malabsorption or severe withdrawal complications. Prevention and treatment of suspected Wernicke encephalopathy require appropriate clinical protocols. Glucose can be given before, after or concurrently; urgent glucose should not be delayed while awaiting thiamine.

Offer peer support and, when consistent with patient preferences, structured professional facilitation of AA participation. In the 2020 Cochrane review, manualized TSF improved continuous abstinence at 12 months compared with other clinical approaches (two studies, 1936 participants; RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.03–1.42). Evidence for drinking intensity and consequences was less certain and generally did not show clear differences. These mostly US, noncoerced studies do not establish equal efficacy of every mutual-help format or an obligation to attend AA.

Platform: Peptide
GLP-1 receptor agonism remains under investigation for AUD. The 2025 phase 2 trial randomized 48 nontreatment-seeking adults with BMI≥23; paired laboratory self-administration analyses involved 25 participants, while weekly drinking models used the randomized sample. Diagnosis

4
DSM-5-TR clinical diagnosis
A problematic pattern causing clinically significant impairment or distress with any two or more of eleven criteria within a year supports diagnosis. Two or three criteria indicate mild, four or five moderate, and six or more severe AUD. Tolerance and withdrawal are optional criteria. Review history, functional impact, other substance use and psychiatric or medical explanations; exposure biomarkers alone do not diagnose AUD.
Show evidence (2 references)
PMID:37844924 SUPPORT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Other
"The diagnosis of AUD can be made when a patient has a problematic pattern of alcohol use over a year that leads to clinically significant impairment or distress, involving at least 2 of the 11 DSM-5-TR criteria."
The guideline states the DSM-5-TR clinical threshold, supporting the diagnostic construct rather than a molecular cause of addiction.
PMID:37844924 SUPPORT REVIEW SYNTHESIS Other
"Patients are diagnosed with mild AUD if they have 2–3 criteria; moderate AUD with 4–5 criteria; and severe AUD with 6 or more criteria."
The DSM-5-TR severity bands count diagnostic criteria, rather than biological subtypes or withdrawal severity.
ICD-11 alcohol diagnoses
ICD-11 distinguishes alcohol dependence and harmful pattern of use; hazardous use is a separately listed health-risk factor. These categories should not be treated as exact synonyms for the DSM-5-TR severity spectrum.
Show evidence (1 reference)

"This review describes and discusses the alcohol diagnoses within this section of ICD-11, including Alcohol Dependence, Harmful Pattern of Use of Alcohol, and entities such as Alcohol Intoxication, Alcohol Withdrawal, and several alcohol-induced mental disorders, and briefly covers Hazardous..."
Authoritative description of the ICD-11 alcohol diagnostic structure.
AUDIT, AUDIT-C and brief screening
Validated questionnaires identify unhealthy or high-risk drinking and prompt a diagnostic interview. Thresholds depend on the population and screening purpose. AUDIT-C assesses consumption, whereas the AUDIT problems subscale used in PAU genetics is a different measure. Neither is a stand-alone molecular or clinical confirmation of AUD.

The guideline provides screening thresholds for hazardous or harmful use, which require clinical follow-up rather than automatic AUD diagnosis.

"Adults and youth who screen positive for high-risk drinking should undergo a diagnostic interview for mild, moderate or severe AUD using the DSM-5-TR criteria"
A positive screen prompts a diagnostic interview, explicitly separating screening from diagnosis.
Withdrawal risk and severity assessment
History of seizures or delirium, current findings, coexisting disease and available support guide the level of care. PAWSS predicts risk in studied medically ill populations; CIWA-Ar measures current withdrawal symptoms and can be confounded by other illness. CIWA-Ar depends on patient report and should not be used to assess delirium.

Clinical Burden

High
AUD can cause substantial functional impairment and exposure-related medical complications. The cited 2016 GBD figures concern all alcohol consumption, not mortality among a cohort with diagnosed AUD. In NESARC-III, 19.8% of adults with lifetime AUD reported ever receiving treatment or help, broadly defined to include mutual-help services; this is a historical survey estimate.

Clinical Trials

clinicaltrials:NCT05520775 PHASE_II COMPLETED
Completed phase 2 trial randomized 48 nontreatment-seeking adults 21–65 with AUD and BMI≥23. Semaglutide 0.25 mg/week for 4 weeks then 0.5 mg/week for 4 weeks preceded the primary laboratory assessment; week 9 dose escalation followed primary collection. Paired laboratory analyses included 25 participants, so this was not a complete-case 48-person primary outcome. Registered calendar-day drinking was null; other weekly quantity/craving outcomes were exploratory.

Experimental Models

1
Neonatal rodent astrocyte TLR4 perturbations PRIMARY_CELL_CULTURE
Highly enriched astrocyte cultures were exposed to ethanol with non-targeting siRNA and LPS-related controls. Rat knockdown experiments used 50 mM ethanol, whereas mouse knockout cultures used 10 mM. Nuclear p65, pERK and inflammatory readouts support TLR4 dependence. Lipopolysaccharide contamination controls were performed, but direct ethanol–TLR4 binding was not resolved.

HDID selected-line aversion and reward assays
Two selected replicates were compared with concurrent heterogeneous-stock controls. Conditioned taste aversion was attenuated at a moderate 2 g/kg ethanol dose but not at 4 g/kg; details varied by replicate and analysis. Regional CRF pharmacology in DID and intermittent-access mice
VTA CRF6–33 and astressin 2-B reduced DID intake under selected doses; co-infusion supported additive modulation. CRF6–33 had no significant VTA effect in IAA and no CeA effect in either paradigm. Only IAA increased withdrawal handling-induced convulsions. Water intake and weight were assessed, but comprehensive locomotor or alternative-reward specificity was not established.

Chronic ethanol exposure in constitutive Tlr4-knockout mice
Starting at 7 weeks, mice received 10% ethanol in drinking water for 5 months; reported intake and blood alcohol concentrations were similar between genotypes. Cortical inflammatory proteins/transcripts, glial immunoreactivity and cleaved caspase-3 were measured. Knockout attenuated outcomes, with residual GFAP response. Neither alcohol seeking, cognition nor neuron-specific death was directly tested.

click to show 
name: Alcohol Use Disorder
creation_date: '2026-08-09T14:40:00Z'
category: Psychiatric
description: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a heterogeneous pattern of alcohol use causing clinically significant impairment or distress. DSM-5-TR diagnosis requires at least two of eleven criteria within a year and grades severity by criterion count; tolerance and withdrawal are possible criteria rather than requirements. Genetic liability, environment, reinforcement, learning and exposure-related adaptations contribute probabilistically. The three-stage addiction framework organizes relevant mechanisms but is not a necessary linear course for every patient. Remission, recurrence and sustained recovery all occur.
disease_term:
  preferred_term: alcohol use disorder
  term:
    id: MONDO:0007079
    label: alcohol dependence
synonyms:
- Alcoholism
- Alcohol dependence
- Alcohol addiction
- Problematic alcohol use
parents:
- Substance Use Disorder
- Mental Health Disorder
notes: The entry uses the DSM-5-TR clinical construct while its MONDO binding is the narrower alcohol dependence term (MONDO:0007079); ICD-11 retains separate harmful-pattern and dependence diagnoses. Studies of dependence, heavy drinking, alcohol preference and problematic alcohol use are identified at their actual scope. Exposure-related organ complications are represented without implying they are diagnostic or inevitable, and detailed liver mechanisms are curated separately in Alcoholic_Liver_Disease. The ASAM, AAFP, StatPearls and two PMC URL references retain their generated titles; the underlying publications are PMID:32511109, PMID:34523874, PMID:28613774, PMID:37934220 and PMID:20554880, respectively. Primary human, animal and cell observations are distinguished from review frameworks and mechanistic hypotheses. Hazardous use is retained as a diagnostic behavior without a specific causal edge; depression is retained as a potentially bidirectional associated finding rather than assigned an unsupported alcohol-to-depression mechanism.

inheritance:
- name: Polygenic (multifactorial) liability
  inheritance_term:
    preferred_term: polygenic inheritance
    term:
      id: HP:0010982
      label: Polygenic inheritance
  description: Liability is polygenic and depends on environmental exposure. Protective ADH1B and ALDH2 alleles affect ethanol metabolism; their effects do not make this a Mendelian disorder. Twin and adoption meta-analysis estimates roughly 50% heritability in the studied populations, with a modest shared-environment component. Heritability is a population variance estimate, not the fraction of an individual case caused by genes.

    supports: SUPPORT

    snippet: AUD is approximately 50% heritable.
    explanation: Meta-analysis of 12 twin and 5 adoption studies gives the reference heritability estimate for AUD liability.

pathophysiology:
- name: Polygenic Liability
  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  description: Common-variant associations contribute to liability rather than determining disease. The 2023 meta-analysis combines 165,952 AUD or dependence cases, controls and AUDIT problems scores in 1,079,947 participants; it is not a cohort of one million diagnosed cases. The 110 variants are the union of within- and cross-ancestry results, and most data are European ancestry. Specific nonmetabolic variant-to-neural causal routes remain unresolved.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:38062264
    reference_title: Multi-ancestry study of the genetics of problematic alcohol use in over 1 million individuals.

      explanation: The union of within- and cross-ancestry signals supports distributed susceptibility; it does not identify a single necessary mechanism of impaired control.
    - reference: PMID:38062264
      reference_title: Multi-ancestry study of the genetics of problematic alcohol use in over 1 million individuals.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: Despite the high genetic correlation between AUD and AUDIT–P, they are not identical traits, which introduces heterogeneity.
      explanation: The authors explicitly distinguish diagnosed AUD from AUDIT-P, limiting disease-specific interpretation of the combined PAU analysis.
- name: Repeated Ethanol Exposure
  biological_scale: ORGANISM
  description: Repeated alcohol intake supplies the exposure for intoxication, neuroadaptation and medical complications. Dose, timing, host susceptibility and environment influence outcomes; exposure alone does not establish AUD. This exposure node is separate from enzymatic metabolism and from the impaired-control phenotype.
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK436003/
    reference_title: 'Alcohol Use Disorder: Screening, Evaluation, and Management - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: The fact that not every person who drinks alcohol will necessarily experience a loss of control and progression to addiction indicates that AUD is not solely driven by exposure to alcohol.
    explanation: The clinical synthesis distinguishes alcohol exposure from the additional susceptibility required for impaired control and addiction.
  chemical_entities:
  - preferred_term: ethanol
    term:
      id: CHEBI:16236
      label: ethanol
  triggers:
  - preferred_term: exposure to alcohol consumption
    term:
      id: ECTO:0001082
      label: exposure to alcohol consumption
  downstream:
  - target: Acute GABA-A Signaling Modulation
    causal_link_type: DIRECT
    description: Ethanol acutely modulates inhibitory GABA-A signaling in neuronal preparations. This pharmacological effect is distinct from chronic receptor redistribution and does not imply identical effects at every receptor subtype.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:25954150
      reference_title: Targeting glutamate uptake to treat alcohol use disorders.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: IN_VITRO
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: DIRECT
      snippet: the acute actions of ethanol are to inhibit glutamatergic activity and potentiate GABAergic activity.
      explanation: The review describes acute enhancement of inhibitory GABA signaling; receptor subtype, cellular compartment and experimental preparation determine the response.
  - target: Acute NMDA Receptor Inhibition
    causal_link_type: DIRECT
    description: Ethanol inhibits NMDA-receptor-mediated calcium influx in the reviewed neuronal experiments; the acute receptor action is separate from chronic glutamate adaptation.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:25954150
      reference_title: Targeting glutamate uptake to treat alcohol use disorders.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: IN_VITRO
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: DIRECT
      snippet: Intracellularly, ethanol inhibits, non-competitively, the NMDAR-mediated calcium influx in the cortex, Acb, amygdala, hippocampus, and VTA (Nie et al., 1994; Wirkner et al., 2000; Roberto et al., 2004; Stobbs et al., 2004; Zhu et al., 2007).
      explanation: The reviewed neuronal experiments identify inhibition of NMDA-mediated calcium influx, supporting the acute receptor effect rather than chronic glutamate depletion.
  - target: Alcohol-Evoked Endogenous Opioid Signaling
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Drinking produces an opioid-sensitive PET ligand-displacement response in human accumbens and orbitofrontal cortex; the intervening release machinery is not resolved by this experiment.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:22238334
      reference_title: Alcohol consumption induces endogenous opioid release in the human orbitofrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: Drinking alcohol induced opioid release in the nucleus accumbens and orbitofrontal cortex, areas of the brain implicated in reward valuation.
      explanation: Human ligand-displacement PET supports alcohol-evoked endogenous opioid release in accumbens and orbitofrontal cortex, without resolving a peptide or downstream dopamine relay.
  - target: Mesolimbic Dopamine Reinforcement
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Alcohol engages mesolimbic reinforcement circuitry through several neuronal and receptor routes; the dopamine synthesis does not establish one exclusive upstream relay.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:25307573
      reference_title: Neurochemical mechanisms of alcohol withdrawal.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: Dopamine, through its actions via mesolimbic and mesocortical pathways, has long been viewed as playing a central role in mediating alcohol reward (Gonzales et al., 2004; Spanagel, 2009).
      explanation: The experimental synthesis assigns mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine a reinforcement role; extension to loss of control requires additional circuit and behavioral steps.
  - target: GABA-A Receptor Redistribution
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Single and repeated ethanol regimens alter receptor trafficking and surface composition in rodents. The exact signaling route and persistence depend on the regimen and neuronal compartment.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:28931433
      reference_title: Role of GABA(A) receptors in alcohol use disorders suggested by chronic intermittent ethanol (CIE) rodent model.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: One-dose ethanol exposure induces transient plastic changes in GABAA receptor subunit levels, composition, and regional and subcellular localization.
      explanation: Rodent exposure experiments summarized here show receptor redistribution after one dose, supporting plasticity without implying permanent or uniform receptor loss.
    - reference: PMID:28931433
      reference_title: Role of GABA(A) receptors in alcohol use disorders suggested by chronic intermittent ethanol (CIE) rodent model.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: One-dose ethanol exposure induces transient plastic changes in GABA A receptor subunit levels, composition, and regional and subcellular localization. ... After chronic intermittent ethanol (CIE) treatment the same changes are observed but they become persistent after 30 or more doses, lasting for at least 120 days in the rat
      explanation: The review distinguishes persistent receptor remodeling after repeated exposure from the reversible single-dose changes; this is a rat result, not a human threshold.
  - target: Altered Glutamate Homeostasis
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Exposure and withdrawal are associated with altered glutamate regulation. Human regional measurements and repeated-vapor rodent experiments do not imply a single uniform trajectory.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:25307573
      reference_title: Neurochemical mechanisms of alcohol withdrawal.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: Some studies have reported reduced cortical glutamate levels associated with dependence and acute withdrawal (Mon et al., 2012; Ende et al., 2013), while other studies have shown elevated glutamate activity in anterior cingulate and striatum in alcohol-dependent subjects (Hermann et al., 2012; Bauer et al., 2013).  # codespell:ignore-line
      explanation: Human measurements differ by brain region and withdrawal timing, supporting altered glutamate regulation rather than a universal increase or decrease.
    - reference: PMID:25307573
      reference_title: Neurochemical mechanisms of alcohol withdrawal.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: Repeated cycles of chronic intermittent exposure to alcohol vapor were shown to increase basal levels of glutamate in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) at time points beyond acute withdrawal.
      explanation: Repeated vapor exposure increases accumbal glutamate in the reviewed rodent experiments beyond the acute withdrawal period.
  - target: CRF-Associated Stress Signaling
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: The withdrawal framework recruits extended-amygdala CRF systems after repeated drug exposure; complete mediation of the human stress response remains unresolved.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:27475769
      reference_title: 'Neurobiology of addiction: a neurocircuitry analysis.'
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: The increases in negative emotional states and dysphoric and stress-like responses in the withdrawal/negative affect stage involve decreases in the function of the dopamine component of the reward system and recruitment of brain stress neurotransmitters, such as corticotropin-releasing factor and dynorphin, in the neurocircuitry of the extended amygdala.
      explanation: The review places CRF, dynorphin and reduced reward signaling within the extended-amygdala withdrawal framework; their contributions are not an obligatory sequence in every patient.
  - target: Dynorphin–Kappa-Opioid Signaling
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Dependent-animal and neurocircuitry evidence implicates dynorphin signaling in withdrawal-related stress, without establishing its recruitment as universal in AUD.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:27475769
      reference_title: 'Neurobiology of addiction: a neurocircuitry analysis.'
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: The increases in negative emotional states and dysphoric and stress-like responses in the withdrawal/negative affect stage involve decreases in the function of the dopamine component of the reward system and recruitment of brain stress neurotransmitters, such as corticotropin-releasing factor and dynorphin, in the neurocircuitry of the extended amygdala.
      explanation: The review places CRF, dynorphin and reduced reward signaling within the extended-amygdala withdrawal framework; their contributions are not an obligatory sequence in every patient.
  - target: Withdrawal-Associated Reward Deficit
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Withdrawal from chronic exposure lowers dopamine activity in reviewed rodent experiments; the transition to a human subjective reward deficit requires additional interpretation.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:25307573
      reference_title: Neurochemical mechanisms of alcohol withdrawal.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: By contrast, withdrawal from chronic alcohol exposure has been reported to result in decreased VTA dopamine neuronal activity (Diana et al., 1996; Bailey et al., 2001), and reduced basal levels of dopamine in ventral and dorsal subregions of the striatum, possibly due to enhanced dopamine uptake (Weiss et al., 1996; Budygin et al., 2007; Barak et al., 2011).
      explanation: The reviewed rodent measurements link withdrawal to reduced VTA firing and striatal dopamine, supporting a reward-deficit model with incompletely resolved behavioral mediation.
  - target: Habitual Alcohol Seeking
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Repeated seeking and reinforcement permit habitual control to develop in the rat paradigm; the predictor relationship does not prove that exposure alone determines later compulsivity.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:33955649
      reference_title: Individual differences in the engagement of habitual control over alcohol seeking predict the development of compulsive alcohol seeking and drinking.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: After seeking behaviour was well established, subjects that had developed greater resistance to outcome devaluation (were more habitual) were more likely to show punishment-resistant (compulsive) alcohol seeking.
      explanation: Outcome-devaluation resistance predicted punishment-resistant seeking in selected rats; the association does not prove that habitual control alone causes human compulsive drinking.
  - target: Thiamine Deficiency
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_KNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Heavy drinking can reduce nutritional intake and impair thiamine availability. These known nutritional intermediates are not expanded into separate nodes here.
    evidence:
    - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
      reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: Patients consuming large volumes of alcohol are at an increased risk of developing Wernicke encephalopathy due to inadequate nutrition as well as biological interactions between cellular functioning and alcohol.
      explanation: The guideline connects heavy drinking with nutritional and biological risks for thiamine-related disease, supporting a conditional deficiency pathway.
  - target: TLR4-Dependent Inflammatory Signaling
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Chronic ethanol exposure produces TLR4-dependent inflammatory responses in mouse and astrocyte models; the experiments do not establish ethanol as a direct TLR4 ligand.
    evidence:
    - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6634595/
      reference_title: Pivotal Role of TLR4 Receptors in Alcohol-Induced Neuroinflammation and Brain Damage - PMC
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: Our findings support the critical role of the TLR4 response in the neuroinflammation, brain injury, and possibly in the neurodegeneration induced by chronic ethanol intake.
      explanation: The mouse study supports receptor dependence of measured inflammatory and injury markers; neurodegeneration was proposed rather than a measured clinical outcome.
  - target: Alcohol Cue Responsivity
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Repeated pairing and learning offer an interpretation of cue-associated responses; the imaging synthesis alone does not prove longitudinal sensitization.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:22574861
      reference_title: 'Functional neuroimaging studies of alcohol cue reactivity: a quantitative meta-analysis and systematic review.'
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: Among cases, alcohol cues elicited robust activation of limbic and prefrontal regions, including ventral striatum, anterior cingulate and ventromedial prefrontal cortex.
      explanation: The human imaging meta-analysis localizes within-case cue responses to ventral striatal and prefrontal circuitry, without equating activation with a causal deficit.
    - reference: PMID:22574861
      reference_title: 'Functional neuroimaging studies of alcohol cue reactivity: a quantitative meta-analysis and systematic review.'
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: Cue-elicited activation of ventral striatum was most frequently correlated with behavioral measures and most frequently reduced by treatment, but these results were often derived from region-of-interest analyses that interrogated only limbic regions.
      explanation: Behavioral correlations and treatment-related changes support cue responsivity as an associative mechanism candidate, while region-of-interest selection limits generalization.
  - target: Impaired Executive Control
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: The framework describes an exposure-associated contribution to executive dysfunction; pre-existing liability and other factors cannot be excluded by cross-sectional imaging.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:27475769
      reference_title: 'Neurobiology of addiction: a neurocircuitry analysis.'
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: The craving and deficits in executive function in the so-called preoccupation/anticipation stage involve the dysregulation of key afferent projections from the prefrontal cortex and insula, including glutamate, to the basal ganglia and extended amygdala.
      explanation: The synthesis links executive-control problems to prefrontal projections, providing circuit context without proving a single lesion causes impaired control.
  - target: Withdrawal-Associated Autonomic Activation
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Withdrawal after sustained heavy exposure can activate autonomic responses in physiologically dependent individuals.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:25307573
      reference_title: Neurochemical mechanisms of alcohol withdrawal.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: Clinical features of alcohol withdrawal include signs of central nervous system hyperexcitability, heightened autonomic nervous system activation, and a constellation of symptoms contributing to psychologic discomfort and negative affect.
      explanation: The human withdrawal syndrome includes both central hyperexcitability and autonomic activation; this clinical description alone does not identify a particular receptor mediator.
  - target: Hepatic Steatosis
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_KNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Alcohol metabolism and disturbed lipid handling connect sustained exposure to hepatic fat accumulation; those known liver-specific intermediates are curated in Alcoholic_Liver_Disease.
    evidence:

      reference_title: Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: Alcoholic Fatty Liver or Steatosis - At this stage, fat accumulates in the liver parenchyma.
      explanation: The clinical review describes hepatic fat accumulation as alcohol-associated steatosis; the detailed metabolic pathway is curated separately.
  - target: Cirrhosis
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_KNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Alcohol-associated liver disease can progress from steatosis through hepatitis to cirrhosis in a subset of patients; the liver-specific intermediate processes are not expanded in this AUD graph.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:31536239
      reference_title: Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: DIRECT
      snippet: The alcoholic liver disease covers a spectrum of disorders beginning from the fatty liver, progressing at times to alcoholic hepatitis and culminating in alcoholic cirrhosis
      explanation: The clinical synthesis describes progression to cirrhosis within alcohol-associated liver disease; progression is conditional, not inevitable.
  - target: Dilated Cardiomyopathy
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_KNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Chronic alcohol toxicity can produce myocardial injury and adverse remodeling before ventricular dilation; the organ-specific intermediates are not expanded here.
    evidence:
    - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK436003/
      reference_title: 'Alcohol Use Disorder: Screening, Evaluation, and Management - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf'
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: Chronic alcohol use can accelerate coronary artery disease and cause dilated cardiomyopathy.
      explanation: The source recognizes dilated cardiomyopathy as a possible consequence of chronic alcohol use, rather than a defining AUD phenotype.
  - target: Pancreatitis
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_KNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Alcohol-related pancreatic injury and inflammation can lead to acute or chronic pancreatitis through organ-specific pathways omitted from this graph.
    evidence:
    - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK436003/
      reference_title: 'Alcohol Use Disorder: Screening, Evaluation, and Management - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf'

      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: In addition to liver disease, alcohol can cause both acute and chronic pancreatitis as well as exocrine insufficiency.
      explanation: The clinical synthesis supports both acute and chronic pancreatitis as alcohol-related complications; it does not assign a population frequency.
  - target: Peripheral Neuropathy
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_KNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Direct neurotoxicity and nutritional injury are recognized routes from chronic alcohol use to peripheral neuropathy; the nerve-specific intermediates are not expanded here.

      directness: INDIRECT

      explanation: The quoted clinical observation supports alcohol-associated small-fiber neuropathy, without implying every neuropathy in an AUD patient has that cause.
  - target: Acetaldehyde Accumulation
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_KNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Ethanol is converted by ADH enzymes to acetaldehyde; accumulation depends on the balance between this known formation step and ALDH-mediated clearance.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:17718394
      reference_title: 'The genetics of alcohol metabolism: role of alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase variants.'
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: IN_VITRO
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: A variant of the ALDH2 gene encodes an essentially inactive ALDH enzyme, resulting in acetaldehyde accumulation
      explanation: Reduced ALDH2 function decreases aldehyde clearance and favors acetaldehyde accumulation during drinking; its association with lower dependence risk is protective.
- name: Increased ADH1B-Mediated Ethanol Oxidation
  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  description: In carriers of protective high-activity ADH1B alleles, faster enzyme-catalyzed conversion of ethanol to acetaldehyde is proposed to contribute to aversive effects and reduced dependence risk. Purified-enzyme kinetics do not imply the same fold change in whole-body clearance or a universal flushing response.

- name: Acute GABA-A Signaling Modulation
  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  description: Acute ethanol can enhance GABAergic inhibition through effects that depend on receptor composition, synaptic compartment, dose and brain region. The review evidence includes rodent and cellular work; it does not establish uniform potentiation at every receptor or a single necessary route to human intoxication. GABAergic neurons supply the inhibitory transmitter; receptor-bearing target neurons need not themselves be GABAergic.

- name: Acute NMDA Receptor Inhibition
  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  description: Experimental literature describes inhibition of NMDA-receptor-mediated calcium influx by ethanol. This acute receptor effect is distinct from chronic changes in receptor trafficking, glutamate release and uptake.
  evidence:

    reference_title: Targeting glutamate uptake to treat alcohol use disorders.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Intracellularly, ethanol inhibits, non-competitively, the NMDAR-mediated calcium influx in the cortex, Acb, amygdala, hippocampus, and VTA (Nie et al., 1994; Wirkner et al., 2000; Roberto et al., 2004; Stobbs et al., 2004; Zhu et al., 2007).
    explanation: The reviewed neuronal experiments identify inhibition of NMDA-mediated calcium influx, supporting the acute receptor effect rather than chronic glutamate depletion.

- name: Alcohol-Evoked Endogenous Opioid Signaling
  biological_scale: CELLULAR
  description: Human positron-emission tomography after drinking showed displacement of a mu-opioid radioligand in nucleus accumbens and orbitofrontal cortex, interpreted as endogenous opioid release. This is an indirect release measure; the study did not identify the peptide, resolve a dopamine relay, or test naltrexone efficacy.
  evidence:

    reference_title: Alcohol consumption induces endogenous opioid release in the human orbitofrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Drinking alcohol induced opioid release in the nucleus accumbens and orbitofrontal cortex, areas of the brain implicated in reward valuation.
    explanation: Human ligand-displacement PET supports alcohol-evoked endogenous opioid release in accumbens and orbitofrontal cortex, without resolving a peptide or downstream dopamine relay.

- name: Mesolimbic Dopamine Reinforcement
  biological_scale: CELLULAR
  description: Mesolimbic dopamine signaling contributes to alcohol reinforcement in the reviewed experimental framework. Dopamine is one contributor among several; the cited human opioid PET result alone does not prove an opioid-to-dopamine causal sequence.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:25307573
    reference_title: Neurochemical mechanisms of alcohol withdrawal.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Dopamine, through its actions via mesolimbic and mesocortical pathways, has long been viewed as playing a central role in mediating alcohol reward (Gonzales et al., 2004; Spanagel, 2009).
    explanation: The experimental synthesis assigns mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine a reinforcement role; extension to loss of control requires additional circuit and behavioral steps.

    term:

- name: Alcohol Cue Responsivity
  biological_scale: TISSUE
  description: Alcohol-associated cues evoke brain responses that can correlate with craving. The meta-analysis included 28 studies of heavy-drinking/AUD samples; within-case ventral-striatal activation was not equivalent to a significant case-versus-control difference. Region-of-interest selection, heterogeneous ascertainment and mainly male samples limit generalization. This is an associative circuit finding, not a validated clinical biomarker.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:22574861
    reference_title: 'Functional neuroimaging studies of alcohol cue reactivity: a quantitative meta-analysis and systematic review.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Among cases, alcohol cues elicited robust activation of limbic and prefrontal regions, including ventral striatum, anterior cingulate and ventromedial prefrontal cortex.
    explanation: The human imaging meta-analysis localizes within-case cue responses to ventral striatal and prefrontal circuitry, without equating activation with a causal deficit.
  - reference: PMID:22574861
    reference_title: 'Functional neuroimaging studies of alcohol cue reactivity: a quantitative meta-analysis and systematic review.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Cue-elicited activation of ventral striatum was most frequently correlated with behavioral measures and most frequently reduced by treatment, but these results were often derived from region-of-interest analyses that interrogated only limbic regions.
    explanation: Behavioral correlations and treatment-related changes support cue responsivity as an associative mechanism candidate, while region-of-interest selection limits generalization.
  downstream:
  - target: Impaired Control over Alcohol Use
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Cue-related circuit responses correlate with behavior, but the imaging synthesis does not prove that those responses cause later loss of control.

- name: GABA-A Receptor Redistribution
  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  description: Rodent chronic-intermittent-ethanol studies and cell/slice assays describe time- and compartment-dependent changes in GABA-A receptor surface composition. Reduced tonic ethanol sensitivity can coexist with increased sensitivity of some synaptic currents. Single-dose changes can reverse, while repeated regimens produce longer persistence; endpoint-specific tolerance is not universal receptor loss or proven lifelong human dysfunction. Hippocampal and cortical pyramidal-neuron recordings are among the preparations supporting these changes.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:28931433
    reference_title: Role of GABA(A) receptors in alcohol use disorders suggested by chronic intermittent ethanol (CIE) rodent model.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: One-dose ethanol exposure induces transient plastic changes in GABAA receptor subunit levels, composition, and regional and subcellular localization.
    explanation: Rodent exposure experiments summarized here show receptor redistribution after one dose, supporting plasticity without implying permanent or uniform receptor loss.
  - reference: PMID:25307573
    reference_title: Neurochemical mechanisms of alcohol withdrawal.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: For example, studies in hippocampal and cortical pyramidal neurons have shown that chronic alcohol exposure reduces the frequency, amplitude, and decay time of mini inhibitory postsynaptic currents, effects that all contribute to increased neural excitability during withdrawal (Fleming et al., 2009).  # codespell:ignore-line
    explanation: The review explicitly identifies hippocampal and cortical pyramidal-neuron recordings as evidence for altered inhibitory currents after chronic exposure.
  - reference: PMID:28931433
    reference_title: Role of GABA(A) receptors in alcohol use disorders suggested by chronic intermittent ethanol (CIE) rodent model.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: INDIRECT
    snippet: One-dose ethanol exposure induces transient plastic changes in GABA A receptor subunit levels, composition, and regional and subcellular localization. ... After chronic intermittent ethanol (CIE) treatment the same changes are observed but they become persistent after 30 or more doses, lasting for at least 120 days in the rat
    explanation: The review distinguishes persistent receptor remodeling after repeated exposure from the reversible single-dose changes; this is a rat result, not a human threshold.
  molecular_functions:
  - preferred_term: GABA-A receptor activity
    term:
      id: GO:0004890
      label: GABA-A receptor activity
  downstream:
  - target: Withdrawal-Associated CNS Hyperexcitability
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_KNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Changes in inhibitory or excitatory synaptic signaling alter neuronal excitability when ethanol is reduced. These known physiological intermediates are summarized here; their relative contribution differs across models and patients.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:28931433
      reference_title: Role of GABA(A) receptors in alcohol use disorders suggested by chronic intermittent ethanol (CIE) rodent model.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: Compensatory up-regulation of synaptically localized α4 and α2 subunit-containing GABAA receptor subtypes, mediating ethanol-sensitive synaptic inhibitory currents follow, but exhibit altered physio-pharmacology, seizure susceptibility, hyperexcitability, anxiety, and tolerance to GABAergic positive allosteric modulators, corresponding to heightened alcohol withdrawal syndrome.
      explanation: The review relates rodent receptor remodeling to altered physiology and withdrawal-related endpoints; this does not establish a uniform human receptor mechanism.
    - reference: PMID:25307573
      reference_title: Neurochemical mechanisms of alcohol withdrawal.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: Clinical features of alcohol withdrawal include signs of central nervous system hyperexcitability, heightened autonomic nervous system activation, and a constellation of symptoms contributing to psychologic discomfort and negative affect.
      explanation: The human withdrawal syndrome includes both central hyperexcitability and autonomic activation; this clinical description alone does not identify a particular receptor mediator.

- name: Altered Glutamate Homeostasis
  biological_scale: CELLULAR
  description: Repeated ethanol exposure and withdrawal can alter glutamate release, uptake and receptor regulation. Elevated extracellular glutamate is supported in particular rodent dependence models, while human spectroscopy results vary by region and timing and do not all show elevation. The whole process should not be reduced to universal NMDA-receptor upregulation.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:25307573
    reference_title: Neurochemical mechanisms of alcohol withdrawal.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Some studies have reported reduced cortical glutamate levels associated with dependence and acute withdrawal (Mon et al., 2012; Ende et al., 2013), while other studies have shown elevated glutamate activity in anterior cingulate and striatum in alcohol-dependent subjects (Hermann et al., 2012; Bauer et al., 2013).  # codespell:ignore-line
    explanation: Human measurements differ by brain region and withdrawal timing, supporting altered glutamate regulation rather than a universal increase or decrease.
  - reference: PMID:25307573
    reference_title: Neurochemical mechanisms of alcohol withdrawal.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Repeated cycles of chronic intermittent exposure to alcohol vapor were shown to increase basal levels of glutamate in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) at time points beyond acute withdrawal.
    explanation: Repeated vapor exposure increases accumbal glutamate in the reviewed rodent experiments beyond the acute withdrawal period.
  biological_processes:
  - preferred_term: synaptic transmission, glutamatergic
    term:
      id: GO:0035249
      label: synaptic transmission, glutamatergic
    modifier: ABNORMAL

    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_KNOWN_INTERMEDIATES

      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: These adaptive changes in NMDA expression and function are suggested to contribute to withdrawal-related CNS hyperexcitability and escalation of drinking and cognitive impairments associated with dependence (Wang et al., 2010; Kroener et al., 2012; Ben Hamida et al., 2013).
      explanation: The review explicitly proposes a contribution of experimentally observed NMDA adaptations to withdrawal hyperexcitability; it does not establish uniform receptor mediation in human AUD.

- name: Withdrawal-Associated CNS Hyperexcitability
  biological_scale: CELLULAR
  description: Reduction or cessation after sustained heavy exposure in a physiologically dependent person can uncover altered inhibitory/excitatory regulation. This contributes to tremor, insomnia, hallucinations and, in severe cases, seizures or delirium. Withdrawal is neither universal in AUD nor a requirement for diagnosis.

- name: Withdrawal-Associated Autonomic Activation

  description: Autonomic activation during withdrawal can produce tachycardia, sweating and elevated blood pressure. This component is separated from cortical excitability because controlling heart rate or blood pressure does not prevent withdrawal seizures or delirium.

    snippet: Clinical signs include sweating, elevated blood pressure, tachycardia, hyperthermia, and hyperactive reflexes.

- name: CRF-Associated Stress Signaling
  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  description: The addiction framework implicates CRF signaling in dependence-related stress and negative affect, with much of the causal evidence from rodent regional pharmacology. This is distinct from the nondependent VTA CRF-binding-protein/CRF2 drinking-in-the-dark experiment; that result is not evidence of central-amygdala CRF1 mediation.

    snippet: The increases in negative emotional states and dysphoric and stress-like responses in the withdrawal/negative affect stage involve decreases in the function of the dopamine component of the reward system and recruitment of brain stress neurotransmitters, such as corticotropin-releasing factor and dynorphin, in the neurocircuitry of the extended amygdala.

  description: Dynorphin and kappa-opioid signaling are implicated in aversion and dependence-related drinking in experimental literature. - name: Withdrawal-Associated Reward Deficit
  biological_scale: TISSUE
  description: Reviewed dependence models show reduced dopamine neuronal activity or basal striatal dopamine during withdrawal. These observations support a reward-deficit hypothesis but should not be generalized to every brain region, exposure phase or individual with AUD.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:25307573
    reference_title: Neurochemical mechanisms of alcohol withdrawal.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: By contrast, withdrawal from chronic alcohol exposure has been reported to result in decreased VTA dopamine neuronal activity (Diana et al., 1996; Bailey et al., 2001), and reduced basal levels of dopamine in ventral and dorsal subregions of the striatum, possibly due to enhanced dopamine uptake (Weiss et al., 1996; Budygin et al., 2007; Barak et al., 2011).
    explanation: The reviewed rodent measurements link withdrawal to reduced VTA firing and striatal dopamine, supporting a reward-deficit model with incompletely resolved behavioral mediation.

- name: Withdrawal-Associated Negative Affect
  biological_scale: ORGANISM
  description: Anxiety, dysphoria and other aversive states can motivate renewed drinking for relief. Hyperkatifeia is a cross-drug heuristic framework integrating reward deficits and stress signaling, not a biomarker or a required stage in every patient. Persistent symptoms also require assessment for independent psychiatric illness.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:33318153
    reference_title: 'Drug Addiction: Hyperkatifeia/Negative Reinforcement as a Framework for Medications Development.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: This review focuses on neurochemical/neurocircuitry dysregulations that contribute to hyperkatifeia, defined as a greater intensity of negative emotional/motivational signs and symptoms during withdrawal from drugs of abuse in the withdrawal/negative affect stage of the addiction cycle.
    explanation: The review defines heightened negative affect during withdrawal and proposes its motivational role; it does not establish a single causal neurochemical route.
  downstream:
  - target: Impaired Control over Alcohol Use
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Relief of aversive withdrawal states can motivate renewed use through negative reinforcement; this does not account for all patterns of impaired control.
    evidence:

      reference_title: 'Drug Addiction: Hyperkatifeia/Negative Reinforcement as a Framework for Medications Development.'
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: OTHER
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      snippet: Hyperkatifeia provides an additional source of motivation for compulsive drug seeking via negative reinforcement.
      explanation: The review explicitly proposes negative reinforcement as a route from aversive withdrawal states to compulsive seeking; its cross-drug framework remains indirect for AUD.
      directness: INDIRECT
  - target: Anxiety
    causal_link_type: DIRECT
    description: Anxiety can be part of an aversive withdrawal state, without implying all independent anxiety disorders arise through this route.

- name: Habitual Alcohol Seeking
  biological_scale: ORGANISM
  description: In alcohol-preferring male rats, devaluation-insensitive seeking predicted subsequent punishment-resistant seeking and quinine-resistant drinking. The cited abstract supplies behavioral evidence; its background anatomical account is not a new direct assay of dorsal-striatal dopamine or proof of the same causal sequence in humans.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:33955649
    reference_title: Individual differences in the engagement of habitual control over alcohol seeking predict the development of compulsive alcohol seeking and drinking.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: After seeking behaviour was well established, subjects that had developed greater resistance to outcome devaluation (were more habitual) were more likely to show punishment-resistant (compulsive) alcohol seeking.
    explanation: Outcome-devaluation resistance predicted punishment-resistant seeking in selected rats; the association does not prove that habitual control alone causes human compulsive drinking.
  downstream:
  - target: Impaired Control over Alcohol Use
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: In the rat paradigm, stronger habitual control predicted punishment-resistant seeking; extrapolation to human impaired control remains indirect.
