- name: Impaired Executive Control
  biological_scale: TISSUE
  description: Reduced inhibitory control and altered decision-making can contribute to difficulty limiting alcohol use in the addiction framework. Cross-sectional MRI differences in AUD provide anatomical associations, not proof that alcohol caused progressive atrophy or that a measured structural difference mediated an executive deficit.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:27475769
    reference_title: 'Neurobiology of addiction: a neurocircuitry analysis.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: The craving and deficits in executive function in the so-called preoccupation/anticipation stage involve the dysregulation of key afferent projections from the prefrontal cortex and insula, including glutamate, to the basal ganglia and extended amygdala.
    explanation: The synthesis links executive-control problems to prefrontal projections, providing circuit context without proving a single lesion causes impaired control.
  - reference: PMID:32643841
    reference_title: How do substance use disorders compare to other psychiatric conditions on structural brain abnormalities? A cross-disorder meta-analytic comparison using the ENIGMA consortium findings.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: INDIRECT
    snippet: On measures of cortical thickness, AUD was associated with significant differences bilaterally in the fusiform gyrus, inferior temporal gyrus, temporal pole, superior frontal gyrus, and rostral and caudal anterior cingulate gyri.
    explanation: Cross-sectional anatomical associations support context for the framework, without directly measuring a causal effect on executive performance.
  downstream:
  - target: Impaired Control over Alcohol Use
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES

- name: Impaired Control over Alcohol Use
  biological_scale: ORGANISM
  description: Impaired control and persistent use despite harm are clinical manifestations to which reinforcement, learned cue responses, aversive-state relief and executive-control problems may contribute. These routes can coexist but are not a mandatory ordered sequence, and DSM criteria allow heterogeneous presentations.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:37844924
    reference_title: Canadian guideline for the clinical management of high-risk drinking and alcohol use disorder.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: The diagnosis of AUD can be made when a patient has a problematic pattern of alcohol use over a year that leads to clinically significant impairment or distress, involving at least 2 of the 11 DSM-5-TR criteria.
    explanation: The guideline states the DSM-5-TR clinical threshold, supporting the diagnostic construct rather than a molecular cause of addiction.

- name: Thiamine Deficiency
  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  description: Poor intake and alcohol-related interference with thiamine handling can produce deficiency and neurologic complications. Nutritional deficiency is an exposure-associated pathway distinct from reinforcement and receptor adaptation; not everyone with AUD develops it.
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Patients consuming large volumes of alcohol are at an increased risk of developing Wernicke encephalopathy due to inadequate nutrition as well as biological interactions between cellular functioning and alcohol.
    explanation: The guideline connects heavy drinking with nutritional and biological risks for thiamine-related disease, supporting a conditional deficiency pathway.
  downstream:
  - target: Memory Impairment
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_KNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Thiamine deficiency can cause metabolic brain injury and region-specific neurologic dysfunction, leading to this manifestation in affected patients.
    evidence:
    - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK436003/
      reference_title: 'Alcohol Use Disorder: Screening, Evaluation, and Management - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf'
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: Chronic alcohol use leading to thiamine deficiency can result in Korsakoff syndrome marked by antero- and retrograde amnesia.
      explanation: The clinical synthesis links thiamine-related Korsakoff syndrome to anterograde and retrograde memory impairment; this is a complication in a subset of patients.
  - target: Ataxia
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_KNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Thiamine deficiency can cause metabolic brain injury and region-specific neurologic dysfunction, leading to this manifestation in affected patients.
    evidence:
    - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
      reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: Patients with thiamine deficiency often present with signs and symptoms such as confusion, abnormal gaze patterns or nystagmus, ataxia, and possibly delirium.
      explanation: The guideline lists ataxia among manifestations of thiamine deficiency, supporting the nutritional complication without making it a general AUD finding.
- name: TLR4-Dependent Inflammatory Signaling
  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  description: In female mice exposed to ethanol for five months and in neonatal rodent astrocyte preparations, Tlr4 deletion or knockdown attenuated inflammatory responses. Direct ethanol binding to TLR4 was not established. The constitutive whole-body knockout does not isolate an astrocyte- or microglia-autonomous mechanism in vivo or prove this pathway causes human AUD.
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6634595/
    reference_title: Pivotal Role of TLR4 Receptors in Alcohol-Induced Neuroinflammation and Brain Damage - PMC
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Our findings support the critical role of the TLR4 response in the neuroinflammation, brain injury, and possibly in the neurodegeneration induced by chronic ethanol intake.
    explanation: The mouse study supports receptor dependence of measured inflammatory and injury markers; neurodegeneration was proposed rather than a measured clinical outcome.
  genes:
  - preferred_term: TLR4
    term:
      id: hgnc:11850
      label: TLR4
  downstream:
  - target: Astrocytic NF-kappa-B Activation
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_KNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: TLR4 signals through intracellular adaptor and kinase pathways to NF-kappa-B. Astrocyte knockdown supports this route, while the intervening canonical signaling steps are not separate graph nodes.
    evidence:
    - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6634595/
      reference_title: Pivotal Role of TLR4 Receptors in Alcohol-Induced Neuroinflammation and Brain Damage - PMC
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: IN_VITRO
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: Gene silencing of TLR4 downregulates the TLR4 expression and reduces NFκB activation induced by ethanol in astrocytes in culture.
      explanation: TLR4 knockdown reduces ethanol-induced NF-kappa-B activation in cultured astrocytes, establishing a perturbation result within that cell preparation.
  - target: Cortical Inflammatory Mediator Induction
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Constitutive Tlr4 deletion prevents the measured cortical cytokine induction in this mouse regimen; cell-specific production and all intervening routes remain unresolved.
    evidence:
    - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6634595/
      reference_title: Pivotal Role of TLR4 Receptors in Alcohol-Induced Neuroinflammation and Brain Damage - PMC
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: chronic ethanol treatment upregulated the levels of TNF-α, IL-1β, and mRNA IL-6 in the cortex homogenates of the WT mice, whereas no changes were observed in the levels of these cytokines in the cerebral cortices of the TLR4-KO mice.
      explanation: The wild-type versus knockout comparison shows TLR4-dependent cortical cytokine changes in mice; homogenate measurements do not identify every producing cell.
  - target: Cortical Glial Reactivity
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Tlr4 deletion attenuates cortical GFAP reactivity but leaves a residual response; the experiment does not isolate every intervening glial signal.
    evidence:
    - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6634595/
      reference_title: Pivotal Role of TLR4 Receptors in Alcohol-Induced Neuroinflammation and Brain Damage - PMC
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: although GFAP immunoreactivity markedly increased (∼16-fold) in the medial frontal cortex of the WT ethanol-treated mice, the levels of this protein only increased ∼3-fold in the TLR4-KO ethanol-treated animals
      explanation: The GFAP increase is attenuated but persists in knockout mice, supporting a partial TLR4 contribution rather than complete prevention of glial reactivity.
  - target: Cortical Caspase-3 Activation
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: The mouse comparison associates TLR4 function with ethanol-induced cortical caspase-3 cleavage; the responsible cell type and intervening death pathway remain unresolved.
    evidence:
    - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6634595/
      reference_title: Pivotal Role of TLR4 Receptors in Alcohol-Induced Neuroinflammation and Brain Damage - PMC
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: the Western blot analysis shows caspase-3 activation as the appearance of the ∼17 kDa caspase-3 cleavage fragment in cerebral cortices of the ethanol-treated WT animals. Conversely, chronic ethanol treatment did not induce caspase-3 activation in the TLR4-KO animals
      explanation: The passage compares ethanol-exposed wild-type and Tlr4-knockout cortices, supporting genotype-dependent caspase-3 activation without identifying a dying cell type.

  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  description: Cleaved caspase-3 and immunoreactivity increased in ethanol-exposed wild-type mouse cortex and were attenuated by Tlr4 deficiency. This supports an injury/apoptosis-associated signal, without directly identifying dying neurons, quantifying cognitive impairment, or proving an inflammatory mediator was the necessary intermediate.
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6634595/
    reference_title: Pivotal Role of TLR4 Receptors in Alcohol-Induced Neuroinflammation and Brain Damage - PMC
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: the Western blot analysis shows caspase-3 activation as the appearance of the ∼17 kDa caspase-3 cleavage fragment in cerebral cortices of the ethanol-treated WT animals. Conversely, chronic ethanol treatment did not induce caspase-3 activation in the TLR4-KO animals
    explanation: The passage compares ethanol-exposed wild-type and Tlr4-knockout cortices, supporting genotype-dependent caspase-3 activation without identifying a dying cell type.
  locations:
  - preferred_term: cerebral cortex
    term:
      id: UBERON:0000956
      label: cerebral cortex
- name: VTA CRF2-Associated Drinking Modulation
  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  description: In male mice, local VTA CRF2 antagonism reduced nondependent drinking-in-the-dark intake; CRF-binding-protein interference added to the effect under tested conditions. The study did not assay dopamine, NMDA currents or physical receptor interactions. CRF-binding-protein blockade was ineffective in central amygdala and in the dependent intermittent-access VTA condition.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:26247973
    reference_title: 'Corticotropin Releasing Factor Binding Protein and CRF2 Receptors in the Ventral Tegmental Area: Modulation of Ethanol Binge Drinking in C57BL/6J Mice.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: These results indicate that VTA CRF2 receptors modulate ethanol binge drinking, and CRFBP may add to the anti-alcohol effect of A2B.
    explanation: Local VTA pharmacology modifies drinking in the nondependent binge paradigm; the result does not establish the same effect in dependence or in all brain regions.
  - reference: PMID:26247973
    reference_title: 'Corticotropin Releasing Factor Binding Protein and CRF2 Receptors in the Ventral Tegmental Area: Modulation of Ethanol Binge Drinking in C57BL/6J Mice.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Intra-CeA CRF6–33 neither affected ethanol binge drinking nor escalated ethanol consumption in mice given IAA.
    explanation: The central-amygdala null result limits regional generalization of the VTA CRF-binding-protein finding.
  downstream:
  - target: Repeated Ethanol Exposure
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Regional pharmacological perturbation altered intake in nondependent DID mice; the intervening neuronal mechanism and human relevance are unresolved.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:26247973
      reference_title: 'Corticotropin Releasing Factor Binding Protein and CRF2 Receptors in the Ventral Tegmental Area: Modulation of Ethanol Binge Drinking in C57BL/6J Mice.'
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: These results indicate that VTA CRF2 receptors modulate ethanol binge drinking, and CRFBP may add to the anti-alcohol effect of A2B.
      explanation: Local VTA pharmacology modifies drinking in the nondependent binge paradigm; the result does not establish the same effect in dependence or in all brain regions.
  locations:
  - preferred_term: ventral tegmental area
    term:
      id: UBERON:0002691
      label: ventral tegmental area
phenotypes:
- category: Behavioral
  name: Addictive Alcohol Use
  description: Impaired control, unsuccessful attempts to reduce use and continued use despite harm may characterize AUD. DSM-5-TR requires a combination of criteria, so no single control symptom or withdrawal finding is mandatory in every case.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Addictive alcohol use
    term:
      id: HP:0030955
      label: Addictive alcohol use
  diagnostic: true
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:37844924
    reference_title: Canadian guideline for the clinical management of high-risk drinking and alcohol use disorder.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: The diagnosis of AUD can be made when a patient has a problematic pattern of alcohol use over a year that leads to clinically significant impairment or distress, involving at least 2 of the 11 DSM-5-TR criteria.
    explanation: The guideline states the DSM-5-TR clinical threshold, supporting the diagnostic construct rather than a molecular cause of addiction.
- category: Behavioral
  name: Problematic Alcohol Consumption
  description: A pattern of drinking causing harm to health or social functioning, graded in DSM-5 as mild (2-3 criteria), moderate (4-5), or severe (6 or more) and separated in ICD-11 into harmful pattern of use versus dependence.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Problematic alcohol consumption
    term:
      id: HP:5200329
      label: Problematic alcohol consumption
  diagnostic: true
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:31194891
    reference_title: 'Alcohol Use Disorders in ICD-11: Past, Present, and Future.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: This review describes and discusses the alcohol diagnoses within this section of ICD-11, including Alcohol Dependence, Harmful Pattern of Use of Alcohol, and entities such as Alcohol Intoxication, Alcohol Withdrawal, and several alcohol-induced mental disorders, and briefly covers Hazardous Alcohol Use, which is listed separately as a health risk factor.
    explanation: Documents the ICD-11 diagnostic structure that grades problematic drinking into harmful use and dependence.
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
  - reference: PMID:37844924
    reference_title: Canadian guideline for the clinical management of high-risk drinking and alcohol use disorder.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: The diagnosis of AUD can be made when a patient has a problematic pattern of alcohol use over a year that leads to clinically significant impairment or distress, involving at least 2 of the 11 DSM-5-TR criteria.
    explanation: The guideline states the DSM-5-TR clinical threshold, supporting the diagnostic construct rather than a molecular cause of addiction.
- category: Behavioral
  name: Craving
  description: A strong desire or urge to use alcohol is one DSM-5-TR criterion and a distinct patient-reported trial outcome. Cue-related imaging is a correlate rather than a diagnostic test or proof of a necessary mechanism.
  notes: 'No `phenotype_term` is bound: HPO has no general craving term (only the food-specific HP:0030083, HP:0030221 and HP:6000785), and using one of those or a generic behavioural parent would misdescribe the claim. Needs term / NTR candidate.'
  diagnostic: true
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:37844924
    reference_title: Canadian guideline for the clinical management of high-risk drinking and alcohol use disorder.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: the patient has troublesome craving (desire or urges) to use alcohol (4)
    explanation: Craving is an explicit DSM-5-TR criterion, but it alone is insufficient for the diagnosis.
- category: Behavioral
  name: Hazardous Alcohol Use
  description: Recurrent use in physically hazardous situations is a possible DSM-5-TR criterion. ICD-11 hazardous use is a separate health-risk category and alone does not establish dependence or AUD.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Hazardous alcohol use
    term:
      id: HP:6000028
      label: Hazardous alcohol use
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:37844924
    reference_title: Canadian guideline for the clinical management of high-risk drinking and alcohol use disorder.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: the patient uses alcohol regularly in situations where it is a hazard to them physically (8)
    explanation: Repeated drinking in physically hazardous situations is a diagnostic criterion, distinct from a proven neural mechanism.
- category: Neurologic
  name: Tremor
  description: Tremor can begin within hours after reduction or cessation of sustained heavy drinking in a physiologically dependent person; timing and severity vary.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Tremor
    term:
      id: HP:0001337
      label: Tremor
    temporality: ACUTE
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0900/p253.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0900/p253.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: leading to tremors, insomnia, nausea and vomiting, hallucinations, anxiety, and agitation.
    explanation: Lists tremor as a core alcohol withdrawal sign.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
- category: Neurologic
  name: Alcohol Withdrawal Seizures
  description: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures can complicate alcohol withdrawal, typically during the first 12–48 hours after cessation or marked reduction. They can occur despite treatment, and assessment must consider other seizure causes.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Generalized tonic-clonic seizure
    term:
      id: HP:0002069
      label: Bilateral tonic-clonic seizure
    temporality: ACUTE
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0900/p253.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0900/p253.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: If untreated or inadequately treated, withdrawal can progress to generalized tonic-clonic seizures, delirium tremens, and death.
    explanation: Identifies withdrawal seizures as a complication of untreated withdrawal.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
- category: Neurologic
  name: Alcohol Withdrawal Delirium
  description: Withdrawal delirium combines disturbed attention and awareness with confusion, often hallucinations and autonomic activation. It is a potentially life-threatening complication requiring close monitoring, and other causes of delirium must also be assessed.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Delirium
    term:
      id: HP:0031258
      label: Delirium
    temporality: ACUTE
    severity: SEVERE
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0900/p253.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0900/p253.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: If untreated or inadequately treated, withdrawal can progress to generalized tonic-clonic seizures, delirium tremens, and death.
    explanation: Establishes delirium tremens as the severe end of the withdrawal spectrum.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
- category: Neurologic
  name: Withdrawal Hallucinations
  description: Visual and tactile hallucinations occurring during alcohol withdrawal, with or without accompanying delirium.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Hallucinations
    term:
      id: HP:0000738
      label: Hallucinations
    temporality: ACUTE
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0900/p253.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0900/p253.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: leading to tremors, insomnia, nausea and vomiting, hallucinations, anxiety, and agitation.
    explanation: Lists hallucinations among the withdrawal manifestations.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
- category: Neurologic
  name: Insomnia
  description: Insomnia can occur during acute withdrawal and may persist during abstinence; it is not specific to AUD.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Insomnia
    term:
      id: HP:0100785
      label: Insomnia
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0900/p253.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0900/p253.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: leading to tremors, insomnia, nausea and vomiting, hallucinations, anxiety, and agitation.
    explanation: Lists insomnia among the withdrawal manifestations.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
  - reference: PMID:25307573
    reference_title: Neurochemical mechanisms of alcohol withdrawal.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: A common complaint among alcoholics is disruption in sleep, which typically emerges during early periods of abstinence and often extends to the more protracted phase of abstinence
    explanation: The clinical review describes sleep disruption during both early and protracted abstinence, supporting the timing of the insomnia claim.
- category: Behavioral
  name: Anxiety
  description: Anxiety can accompany withdrawal or the negative-affect component of dependence; independent anxiety disorders may also coexist. Persistence and mechanisms vary among individuals.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Anxiety
    term:
      id: HP:0000739
      label: Anxiety
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0900/p253.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0900/p253.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: leading to tremors, insomnia, nausea and vomiting, hallucinations, anxiety, and agitation.
    explanation: Documents anxiety as an acute withdrawal feature.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
  - reference: PMID:27475769
    reference_title: 'Neurobiology of addiction: a neurocircuitry analysis.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Drug addiction can be defined as a chronically relapsing disorder, characterised by compulsion to seek and take the drug, loss of control in limiting intake, and emergence of a negative emotional state (eg, dysphoria, anxiety, irritability) when access to the drug is prevented.
    explanation: Supports anxiety as part of the negative emotional state beyond acute withdrawal.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
- category: Constitutional
  name: Withdrawal Tachycardia
  description: Increased heart rate can accompany alcohol withdrawal. This finding is separated from hypertension and sweating rather than using a tachycardia term for the whole autonomic syndrome.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Tachycardia
    term:
      id: HP:0001649
      label: Tachycardia
    temporality: ACUTE
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Clinical signs include sweating, elevated blood pressure, tachycardia, hyperthermia, and hyperactive reflexes.
    explanation: The guideline explicitly lists sweating, tachycardia and elevated blood pressure among withdrawal signs, supporting the autonomic branch.
- category: Gastrointestinal
  name: Nausea and Vomiting
  description: Gastrointestinal upset during alcohol withdrawal.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Nausea and vomiting
    term:
      id: HP:0002017
      label: Nausea and vomiting
    temporality: ACUTE
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0900/p253.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2021/0900/p253.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: leading to tremors, insomnia, nausea and vomiting, hallucinations, anxiety, and agitation.
    explanation: Lists nausea and vomiting among withdrawal manifestations.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
- category: Behavioral
  name: Depression
  description: Depressed mood and independent depressive disorders may coexist with AUD. NESARC-III reports cross-sectional psychiatric associations. The five-year study was ascertained for major depressive disorder (269 patients, 66 with AUD), so it does not estimate depression prevalence among all people with AUD or prove alcohol caused depression.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Depression
    term:
      id: HP:0000716
      label: Depression
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:32217228
    reference_title: 'Comorbid alcohol use disorder in psychiatric MDD patients: A five-year prospective study.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Patients with AUD spent more time depressed and had more suicide attempts during follow-up.
    explanation: Five-year prospective psychiatric cohort links comorbid AUD to a worse depressive course.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
  - reference: PMID:26039070
    reference_title: 'Epidemiology of DSM-5 Alcohol Use Disorder: Results From the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions III.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Significant associations were found between 12-month and lifetime AUD and other substance use disorders, major depressive and bipolar I disorders, and antisocial and borderline personality disorders across all levels of AUD severity, with odds ratios ranging from 1.2 (95% CI, 1.08-1.36) to 6.4 (95% CI, 5.76-7.22).
    explanation: Nationally representative data quantify the association between AUD and major depressive disorder.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
- category: Neurologic
  name: Impaired Executive Functioning
  description: Difficulties with inhibitory control and decision-making are described in addiction models and some patients with AUD. Their extent, timing and contribution to drinking vary; cross-sectional brain anatomy alone does not establish cognitive dysfunction or its causal direction.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Impaired executive functioning
    term:
      id: HP:0033051
      label: Impaired executive functioning
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:27475769
    reference_title: 'Neurobiology of addiction: a neurocircuitry analysis.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: The craving and deficits in executive function in the so-called preoccupation/anticipation stage involve the dysregulation of key afferent projections from the prefrontal cortex and insula, including glutamate, to the basal ganglia and extended amygdala.
    explanation: Identifies executive dysfunction as a defined domain of the addiction cycle.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
- category: Neurologic
  name: Memory Impairment
  description: Memory impairment can be a complication of thiamine deficiency and Korsakoff syndrome in people with sustained heavy alcohol use. It is not a necessary feature of AUD.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Memory impairment
    term:
      id: HP:0002354
      label: Memory impairment
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK436003/
    reference_title: 'Alcohol Use Disorder: Screening, Evaluation, and Management - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Chronic alcohol use leading to thiamine deficiency can result in Korsakoff syndrome marked by antero- and retrograde amnesia.
    explanation: The clinical synthesis links thiamine-related Korsakoff syndrome to anterograde and retrograde memory impairment; this is a complication in a subset of patients.
- category: Neurologic
  name: Ataxia
  description: Ataxia may occur in the setting of alcohol-associated thiamine deficiency and Wernicke encephalopathy; assess nutritional and other neurologic causes rather than attributing every gait problem to AUD.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Ataxia
    term:
      id: HP:0001251
      label: Ataxia
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Patients with thiamine deficiency often present with signs and symptoms such as confusion, abnormal gaze patterns or nystagmus, ataxia, and possibly delirium.
    explanation: The guideline lists ataxia among manifestations of thiamine deficiency, supporting the nutritional complication without making it a general AUD finding.
- category: Neurologic
  name: Peripheral Neuropathy
  description: Peripheral neuropathy may complicate chronic alcohol exposure, with contributions from direct toxicity and nutritional problems varying by patient. The cited clinical chapter describes small-fiber involvement and a stocking-glove distribution.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Peripheral neuropathy
    term:
      id: HP:0009830
      label: Peripheral neuropathy
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK436003/
    reference_title: 'Alcohol Use Disorder: Screening, Evaluation, and Management - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Alcohol can also cause peripheral neuropathy of small fibers
    explanation: The quoted clinical observation supports alcohol-associated small-fiber neuropathy, without implying every neuropathy in an AUD patient has that cause.
- category: Gastrointestinal
  name: Hepatic Steatosis
  description: Hepatic fat accumulation is an early alcohol-associated liver lesion. Progression to hepatitis or cirrhosis occurs in a subset; this is an exposure complication rather than an AUD diagnostic criterion.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Hepatic steatosis
    term:
      id: HP:0001397
      label: Hepatic steatosis
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:31536239
    reference_title: Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Alcoholic Fatty Liver or Steatosis - At this stage, fat accumulates in the liver parenchyma.
    explanation: The clinical review describes hepatic fat accumulation as alcohol-associated steatosis; the detailed metabolic pathway is curated separately.
- category: Gastrointestinal
  name: Cirrhosis
  description: Cirrhosis can develop as an alcohol-associated liver complication in a subset of people with sustained heavy drinking. Its occurrence depends on exposure and host factors and is not part of the AUD diagnostic criteria.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Cirrhosis
    term:
      id: HP:0001394
      label: Cirrhosis
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:31536239
    reference_title: Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: The alcoholic liver disease covers a spectrum of disorders beginning from the fatty liver, progressing at times to alcoholic hepatitis and culminating in alcoholic cirrhosis
    explanation: The clinical synthesis describes progression to cirrhosis within alcohol-associated liver disease; progression is conditional, not inevitable.
- category: Cardiovascular
  name: Dilated Cardiomyopathy
  description: Alcoholic cardiomyopathy from sustained heavy alcohol exposure.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Dilated cardiomyopathy
    term:
      id: HP:0001644
      label: Dilated cardiomyopathy
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK436003/
    reference_title: 'Alcohol Use Disorder: Screening, Evaluation, and Management - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Chronic alcohol use can accelerate coronary artery disease and cause dilated cardiomyopathy.
    explanation: The source recognizes dilated cardiomyopathy as a possible consequence of chronic alcohol use, rather than a defining AUD phenotype.
- category: Gastrointestinal
  name: Pancreatitis
  description: Acute and chronic pancreatitis precipitated by heavy alcohol use.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Pancreatitis
    term:
      id: HP:0001733
      label: Pancreatitis
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK436003/
    reference_title: 'Alcohol Use Disorder: Screening, Evaluation, and Management - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: In addition to liver disease, alcohol can cause both acute and chronic pancreatitis as well as exocrine insufficiency.
    explanation: The clinical synthesis supports both acute and chronic pancreatitis as alcohol-related complications; it does not assign a population frequency.
- category: Constitutional
  name: Facial Flushing After Alcohol Intake
  description: Acetaldehyde-associated flushing, particularly with reduced ALDH2 activity, is an exposure response associated with lower dependence risk rather than a required or typical feature of established AUD. Protection is probabilistic; ADH1B-associated protection should not be equated with a universal systemic flush reaction.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: Facial flushing after alcohol intake
    term:
      id: HP:0001033
      label: Facial flushing after alcohol intake
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:17718394
    reference_title: 'The genetics of alcohol metabolism: role of alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase variants.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Acetaldehyde is a toxic substance whose accumulation leads to a highly aversive reaction that includes facial flushing, nausea, and rapid heart beat (i.e., tachycardia).
    explanation: Ties the flushing phenotype to acetaldehyde accumulation.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS

genetic:
- name: ADH1B
  gene_term:
    preferred_term: ADH1B
    term:
      id: hgnc:250
      label: ADH1B
  relationship_type: PROTECTIVE
  association: ADH1B*2 (rs1229984, His48) encodes an enzyme with increased ethanol-oxidizing activity and is associated with lower alcohol-dependence risk. Purified-enzyme turnover is not a fixed multiplier of whole-body clearance. The proposed aversive mechanism and magnitude of protection vary with genetic and environmental context.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:17718394
    reference_title: 'The genetics of alcohol metabolism: role of alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase variants.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: The ADH1B*2 allele, which is associated with particularly rapid ethanol oxidation, has shown protective effects against alcohol dependence in a variety of populations.
    explanation: The review summarizes human protective associations for ADH1B*2, separate from the purified-enzyme kinetics cited in the mechanism branch.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS

    reference_title: Meta-analyses of ALDH2 and ADH1B with alcohol dependence in Asians.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Recruitment strategy and gender moderated the effect of ADH1B*2.
    explanation: Meta-analysis of ADH1B in Asian populations establishes the association and identifies moderators of its magnitude.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
- name: ALDH2
  gene_term:
    preferred_term: ALDH2
    term:
      id: hgnc:404
      label: ALDH2
  relationship_type: PROTECTIVE
  association: ALDH2*2 (rs671, Glu504Lys in the precursor protein) markedly reduces mitochondrial acetaldehyde clearance, promoting acetaldehyde accumulation and aversive symptoms after alcohol. It is strongly associated with lower dependence risk, especially in studied East Asian populations; neither ancestry nor genotype makes AUD impossible.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:17718394
    reference_title: 'The genetics of alcohol metabolism: role of alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase variants.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL

    explanation: The reviewed human genetic observations support a protective ALDH2*2 association; allele-specific enzyme dysfunction is represented separately.

    snippet: Thirty-one SNPs in GABRA2, but only 1 of the 20 SNPs in the flanking genes, showed significant association with alcoholism.

  association: The 2023 PAU GWAS confirms association of rs1799971 (A118G), distinct from the question of genotype-guided naltrexone treatment. Earlier pharmacogenetic proposals remain unvalidated for routine selection; the cited 147-person head-to-head trial found no genotype treatment interaction, which does not exclude every possible subgroup effect.

  - reference: PMID:38062264

    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: 'Among the 85 regions, there were 5 credible sets that include only a single variant with PIP ≥99% (presumably indicating successful identification of specific causal variants): rs1260326 in GCKR, rs472140 and rs1229984 in ADH1B, rs2699453 (intergenic) and rs2098112 (intergenic).'

  evidence:

environmental:
- name: Alcohol consumption
  description: Alcohol intake supplies the exposure required for alcohol-related reinforcement and complications. Repeated heavy exposure can produce receptor adaptations in experimental paradigms, but exposure does not inevitably lead to AUD. Effects depend on dose, timing and host context.
  effect: Exposure required for alcohol-related effects; insufficient alone to establish AUD
  exposure_term:
    preferred_term: exposure to alcohol consumption
    term:
      id: ECTO:0001082
      label: exposure to alcohol consumption
  chemicals:
  - ethanol
  influences_mechanisms:
  - target: Repeated Ethanol Exposure
    environmental_effect: TRIGGERS
    causal_link_type: DIRECT
    description: Repeated consumption supplies ethanol exposure.
  - target: GABA-A Receptor Redistribution
    environmental_effect: TRIGGERS
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    description: Repeated exposure promotes longer-lasting receptor remodeling in reviewed rodent protocols; the intermediate steps and human time course are unresolved.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:28931433
      reference_title: Role of GABA(A) receptors in alcohol use disorders suggested by chronic intermittent ethanol (CIE) rodent model.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: After chronic intermittent ethanol (CIE) treatment the same changes are observed but they become persistent after 30 or more doses, lasting for at least 120 days in the rat
      explanation: The reviewed rat regimen produces persistent receptor changes after repeated doses; the observation should not be generalized to all human drinking histories.
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK436003/
    reference_title: 'Alcohol Use Disorder: Screening, Evaluation, and Management - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: The fact that not every person who drinks alcohol will necessarily experience a loss of control and progression to addiction indicates that AUD is not solely driven by exposure to alcohol.
    explanation: The clinical synthesis distinguishes alcohol exposure from the additional susceptibility required for impaired control and addiction.
treatments:
- name: Oral Naltrexone
  description: First-line opioid-receptor antagonist for adults with moderate to severe AUD seeking abstinence or reduced drinking. Oral 50 mg/day has the strongest formulation-specific trial evidence for reducing return to heavy drinking; pair with appropriate psychosocial support and patient-defined goals. Current opioid use and acute hepatitis or liver failure are important contraindications; assess future opioid analgesia needs.
  therapeutic_modality: SMALL_MOLECULE
  treatment_term:
    preferred_term: Pharmacotherapy
    term:
      id: NCIT:C15986
      label: Pharmacotherapy
    therapeutic_agent:
    - preferred_term: naltrexone
      term:
        id: CHEBI:7465
        label: naltrexone
  notes: Nausea, vomiting and dizziness can occur. Comparative trials did not establish universal superiority over acamprosate. Benefits concern consumption endpoints; evidence for mortality and other long-term health outcomes is limited.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:37844924
    reference_title: Canadian guideline for the clinical management of high-risk drinking and alcohol use disorder.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: Adult patients with moderate to severe AUD should be offered naltrexone or acamprosate as a first-line pharmacotherapy to support achievement of patient-identified treatment goals.
    explanation: The guideline recommends naltrexone or acamprosate as first-line options for adults with moderate to severe AUD, selected with the patient's goals.

    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Compared with placebo, oral naltrexone (50 mg/d) was associated with lower rates of return to heavy drinking, with a number needed to treat of 11 (95% CI, 5-41).
    explanation: Pooled placebo-controlled human trials support oral 50-mg naltrexone for reducing return to heavy drinking; the estimate is specific to that outcome and formulation.
  - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK436003/

- name: Acamprosate
  description: First-line medication for an abstinence goal, generally started after withdrawal and abstinence. Trial evidence supports reduced return to any drinking, without a clear benefit for preventing return to heavy drinking. The molecular mechanism remains uncertain; it is not curated as a proven reversal of a particular glutamate abnormality. Severe renal impairment is a contraindication and moderate impairment requires dose adjustment.

- name: Disulfiram
  description: An aldehyde-dehydrogenase inhibitor used as an aversive deterrent in selected patients pursuing abstinence. Informed agreement and support or observed dosing are important; drinking while taking it can cause a hazardous reaction. Supervised/open-label studies and blinded efficacy studies have different limitations. Avoid overstating comparative benefit from network estimates.

  treatment_term:

- name: Topiramate
  description: An off-label alternative when first-line medication is ineffective, contraindicated or not preferred. The Canadian guideline gives a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence; systematic review supports reduced consumption endpoints. Cognitive slowing, language difficulties, paresthesias and other adverse effects require consideration. A 147-person 12-week comparison with naltrexone did not establish formal equivalence or superiority on its primary heavy-drinking outcome.
  therapeutic_modality: SMALL_MOLECULE
  treatment_term:
    preferred_term: Pharmacotherapy
    term:
      id: NCIT:C15986

    reference_title: Canadian guideline for the clinical management of high-risk drinking and alcohol use disorder.

    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: Adult patients with moderate to severe AUD who do not benefit from, have contraindications to, or express a preference for an alternate to first-line medications can be offered topiramate or gabapentin.
    explanation: The guideline places topiramate and gabapentin after first-line options are unsuitable or not preferred, rather than making them universal initial treatment.

    explanation: Pooled trial adverse-event findings support counseling about topiramate's cognitive, sensory and other tolerability effects.

    reference_title: 'Topiramate Versus Naltrexone for Alcohol Use Disorder: A Genotype-Stratified Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial.'

    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: For the number of heavy drinking days per week, there was a near-significant time-by-treatment interaction. For the number of standard drinks per drinking day per week, there was a significant time-by-treatment interaction, which favored topiramate.
    explanation: The primary heavy-drinking-day comparison did not reach significance; the secondary drinks-per-drinking-day result favored topiramate. Neither result establishes formal equivalence.
- name: Gabapentin
  description: An off-label alternative for ongoing AUD care when first-line agents are unsuitable, with a conditional recommendation and low-certainty evidence in the Canadian guideline. Sedation, dizziness, renal function and concurrent opioids or other depressants matter. Use for ongoing AUD and use in selected mild withdrawal are separate indications; it does not replace monitored treatment for high-risk withdrawal.

    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: There is insufficient evidence to support the use of baclofen for the treatment of alcohol withdrawal.
    explanation: The withdrawal guideline finds insufficient supporting evidence for baclofen in acute withdrawal, a different indication from ongoing AUD treatment.
- name: Benzodiazepine Withdrawal Management
  description: First-line medication for moderate to severe alcohol withdrawal and prevention or treatment of withdrawal seizures and delirium, with monitoring for oversedation and respiratory depression. Symptom-triggered protocols require reliable assessment; fixed or front-loading approaches may be appropriate. Agent selection and dosing depend on liver function, comorbidity and setting. This is a short-course withdrawal treatment, not ongoing AUD pharmacotherapy.
  therapeutic_modality: SMALL_MOLECULE
  treatment_term:
    preferred_term: Pharmacotherapy
    term:
      id: NCIT:C15986
      label: Pharmacotherapy
    therapeutic_agent:
    - preferred_term: benzodiazepine
      term:
        id: NCIT:C1012
        label: Benzodiazepine
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Benzodiazepines are first-line treatment because of their well-documented effectiveness in reducing the signs and symptoms of withdrawal including the incidence of seizure and delirium.
    explanation: The guideline's synthesis of clinical treatment evidence supports benzodiazepines for withdrawal symptoms and prevention of seizures and delirium.
  - reference: PMID:37844924
    reference_title: Canadian guideline for the clinical management of high-risk drinking and alcohol use disorder.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: Benzodiazepines should not be prescribed as ongoing treatment for AUD
    explanation: The guideline separates short withdrawal treatment from ongoing prescribing for AUD and advises against the latter.
  target_mechanisms:
  - target: Withdrawal-Associated CNS Hyperexcitability
    treatment_effect: INHIBITS
    description: Enhancing inhibitory signaling controls withdrawal and reduces severe complications; ongoing relapse prevention requires additional care.
    evidence:
    - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
      reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: INDIRECT
      snippet: Benzodiazepines are first-line treatment because of their well-documented effectiveness in reducing the signs and symptoms of withdrawal including the incidence of seizure and delirium.
      explanation: The guideline's synthesis of clinical treatment evidence supports benzodiazepines for withdrawal symptoms and prevention of seizures and delirium.
- name: Thiamine Repletion
  description: Give thiamine promptly to prevent or treat deficiency-related neurologic injury. ASAM favors parenteral administration for poor nutrition, malabsorption or severe withdrawal complications. Prevention and treatment of suspected Wernicke encephalopathy require appropriate clinical protocols. Glucose can be given before, after or concurrently; urgent glucose should not be delayed while awaiting thiamine.
  therapeutic_modality: SMALL_MOLECULE
  treatment_term:
    preferred_term: Supportive Care
    term:
      id: NCIT:C15747
      label: Supportive Care
    therapeutic_agent:
    - preferred_term: thiamine
      term:
        id: CHEBI:18385
        label: thiamine(1+)
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: Thiamine should be provided to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
    explanation: The guideline recommends replacement to prevent thiamine-related encephalopathy in the withdrawal-care setting.
  - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: it is important that glucose delivery not be delayed in patients who are nutritionally compromised.
    explanation: The recommendation explicitly prioritizes timely glucose delivery when needed, correcting a rigid thiamine-before-glucose sequence.
  - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: these could be provided in any order or concurrently in order to not delay treatment.
    explanation: The guideline permits concurrent administration or either order, supporting prompt treatment of both nutritional risks.
  target_mechanisms:
  - target: Thiamine Deficiency
    treatment_effect: INHIBITS
    description: Replenishes a deficient vitamin to prevent or treat its complications; it does not directly treat reinforcement or craving.
