      evidence_source: OTHER
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      snippet: Thiamine should be provided to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
      explanation: The guideline recommends replacement to prevent thiamine-related encephalopathy in the withdrawal-care setting.
- name: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy
  description: Structured therapy addresses coping, drinking-related cognitions and relapse prevention. The cited 30-trial meta-analysis included alcohol and other drug disorders; effects were larger against minimal care than against active treatments, with early benefits against nonspecific controls less clear at later follow-up. Lack of a significant difference from another active therapy is not formal equivalence.
  therapeutic_modality: BEHAVIORAL
  treatment_term:
    preferred_term: Cognitive Behavior Therapy
    term:
      id: NCIT:C64345
      label: Cognitive Behavior Therapy
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:31599606
    reference_title: 'A meta-analysis of cognitive-behavioral therapy for alcohol or other drug use disorders: Treatment efficacy by contrast condition.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: The current meta-analysis shows that CBT is more effective than a no treatment, minimal treatment, or nonspecific control.
    explanation: The human trial meta-analysis favors CBT over minimal or nonspecific care, rather than demonstrating superiority over every active therapy.
  - reference: PMID:31599606
    reference_title: 'A meta-analysis of cognitive-behavioral therapy for alcohol or other drug use disorders: Treatment efficacy by contrast condition.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: CBT effects in contrast to a specific therapy were consistently nonsignificant across outcomes and follow-up time points.
    explanation: The same analysis found no consistent advantage over specific active therapies, qualifying the comparative claim for CBT.
- name: Alcoholics Anonymous and Twelve-Step Facilitation
  description: Offer peer support and, when consistent with patient preferences, structured professional facilitation of AA participation. In the 2020 Cochrane review, manualized TSF improved continuous abstinence at 12 months compared with other clinical approaches (two studies, 1936 participants; RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.03–1.42). Evidence for drinking intensity and consequences was less certain and generally did not show clear differences. These mostly US, noncoerced studies do not establish equal efficacy of every mutual-help format or an obligation to attend AA.
  therapeutic_modality: BEHAVIORAL
  treatment_term:
    preferred_term: Behavioral Counseling
    term:
      id: NCIT:C181743
      label: Behavioral Counseling
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:32159228
    reference_title: Alcoholics Anonymous and other 12-step programs for alcohol use disorder.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: RCTs comparing manualized AA/TSF to other clinical interventions (e.g. CBT), showed AA/TSF improves rates of continuous abstinence at 12 months (risk ratio (RR) 1.21, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.03 to 1.42; 2 studies, 1936 participants; high-certainty evidence).
    explanation: The pooled randomized trials support manualized AA/TSF for continuous abstinence at 12 months, with an endpoint- and comparator-specific effect.
  - reference: PMID:32159228
    reference_title: Alcoholics Anonymous and other 12-step programs for alcohol use disorder.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: If people with AUD are opposed to attending AA, despite the strong evidence for its potential to aid recovery, clinicians might consider linkage to alternative mutual‐help organizations as they may confer benefits at similar levels of engagement.
    explanation: The review recommends alternatives when AA is not acceptable; this is a care preference statement rather than a direct equivalence trial of all mutual-help groups.
  notes: The review found no measured quality-of-life or psychological-well-being outcomes. Proposed coping and social-network mechanisms and temporal mediation analyses do not demonstrate normalization of a specific brain circuit.
- name: Semaglutide (investigational)
  description: GLP-1 receptor agonism remains under investigation for AUD. The 2025 phase 2 trial randomized 48 nontreatment-seeking adults with BMI≥23; paired laboratory self-administration analyses involved 25 participants, while weekly drinking models used the randomized sample. Drinks per calendar day and number of drinking days did not significantly improve; craving and drinks per drinking day were exploratory findings. A separate 26-week trial randomized 108 treatment-seeking adults with moderate/severe AUD and obesity to semaglutide or placebo plus CBT, finding a 13.7-percentage-point adjusted between-group reduction in heavy-drinking days.
  therapeutic_modality: PEPTIDE
  treatment_term:
    preferred_term: Pharmacotherapy
    term:
      id: NCIT:C15986
      label: Pharmacotherapy
    therapeutic_agent:
    - preferred_term: semaglutide
      term:
        id: CHEBI:167574
        label: semaglutide
  notes: These selected phase 2 populations and short-term results do not establish general effectiveness, comparative superiority to first-line AUD drugs or a human reward-circuit mechanism. The 2026 result is curated from the available abstract; 88/108 completed and the primary analysis used intention-to-treat with multiple imputation. Gastrointestinal effects and weight loss are relevant.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:39937469
    reference_title: 'Once-Weekly Semaglutide in Adults With Alcohol Use Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Semaglutide treatment did not affect average drinks per calendar day or number of drinking days, but significantly reduced drinks per drinking day
    explanation: The small randomized trial found an effect on drinks per drinking day but not all consumption endpoints, limiting a blanket efficacy claim.
  - reference: PMID:42070571
    reference_title: 'Once-weekly semaglutide versus placebo in patients with alcohol use disorder and comorbid obesity: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Semaglutide was associated with a reduction in heavy drinking days (-41·1 percentage points from baseline, 95% CI -48·7 to -33·5) compared with placebo (-26·4, -34·1 to -18·6; estimated treatment difference -13·7 percentage points, -22·0 to -5·4; p=0·0015), and had substantial effects on multiple secondary alcohol-related and somatic outcomes.
    explanation: A 26-week randomized placebo-controlled trial quantifies the reduction in heavy drinking days in patients with AUD and comorbid obesity.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
- name: Shared-Decision Ongoing AUD Care
  description: Develop a plan around patient goals, which may include abstinence or reduced drinking, and integrate medical, psychiatric and social needs. Offer ongoing care after withdrawal and adjust treatment as circumstances change.
  therapeutic_modality: BEHAVIORAL
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:37844924
    reference_title: Canadian guideline for the clinical management of high-risk drinking and alcohol use disorder.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: All patients who complete withdrawal management should be offered ongoing AUD care.
    explanation: The guideline distinguishes completing withdrawal from treating AUD and recommends continued care after stabilization.
  - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK436003/
    reference_title: 'Alcohol Use Disorder: Screening, Evaluation, and Management - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: Goal setting may include abstinence or reduction in drinking.
    explanation: The clinical guidance permits abstinence or reduction goals, supporting individualized shared decisions.
- name: Brief Motivational Intervention
  description: Offer a brief collaborative intervention after high-risk screening or diagnosis to discuss concerns, goals and treatment options. Its evidence in unhealthy drinking should not be mistaken for adequate stand-alone treatment of every severe AUD presentation.
  therapeutic_modality: BEHAVIORAL
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:37844924
    reference_title: Canadian guideline for the clinical management of high-risk drinking and alcohol use disorder.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: All patients who screen positive for high-risk alcohol use should be offered brief intervention
    explanation: The guideline recommends brief intervention after a positive high-risk screen; screening positivity alone is not a diagnosis of AUD.
- name: Specialist Psychosocial and Family Support
  description: Offer access to structured psychosocial treatment, including family-based approaches where appropriate and acceptable to the patient. Support social needs and referrals alongside medication rather than making medication access depend on participation in a single therapy format.
  therapeutic_modality: BEHAVIORAL
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:37844924
    reference_title: Canadian guideline for the clinical management of high-risk drinking and alcohol use disorder.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: Adult and youth patients with mild to severe AUD should be offered information about and referrals to specialist-led psychosocial treatment interventions in the community
    explanation: The recommendation supports referral to structured psychosocial care across youth and adult AUD populations.
- name: Monitored Withdrawal and Level-of-Care Selection
  description: Assess prior complicated withdrawal, current symptoms, medical/psychiatric illness and home support. Ambulatory care is for appropriately selected patients with reassessment; severe or complicated withdrawal requires an adequately monitored setting. Withdrawal management should connect directly to ongoing AUD care.
  therapeutic_modality: OTHER
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: Most withdrawal severity scales reflect current signs and symptoms and should not be used alone to determine level of care.
    explanation: A current symptom score is not a complete risk or placement assessment, supporting the additional clinical factors described here.
  - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: should be provided close nursing observation and supportive care, which often necessitates admission to an intensive or critical care unit.
    explanation: The recommendation links withdrawal delirium to close observation and often critical care, rather than routine unsupervised management.
- name: Selected Nonbenzodiazepine Withdrawal Options
  description: Gabapentin or carbamazepine can be considered for selected mild withdrawal at low risk of complications. Phenobarbital is an alternative or adjunct for experienced clinicians with appropriate monitoring; parenteral use requires highly supervised care because of oversedation and respiratory risk.
  therapeutic_modality: SMALL_MOLECULE
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: Phenobarbital can be used for some patients in inpatient settings; however, it should only be used by clinicians experienced with its use given its narrow therapeutic window and side effects.
    explanation: The guideline restricts phenobarbital use to suitably experienced clinicians and settings because of its therapeutic window and adverse effects.
- name: Adjunct Control of Withdrawal Autonomic Symptoms
  description: Alpha-2 agonists or beta-blockers may be added for persistent autonomic symptoms in selected patients. They do not prevent or treat withdrawal seizures or delirium and must not replace effective withdrawal therapy.
  therapeutic_modality: SMALL_MOLECULE
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: Alpha2-adrenergic agonists (AA2 s) such as clonidine and dexmedetomidine can be used as an adjunct to benzodiazepine therapy to control autonomic hyperactivity and anxiety when these signs are not controlled by benzodiazepines alone. They should not be used alone to prevent or treat withdrawal-related seizures or delirium.
    explanation: ASAM recommends alpha-2 agonists for adjunctive control of autonomic hyperactivity and anxiety, while explicitly excluding their use alone for seizures or delirium.
  - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: Beta-adrenergic antagonists (beta-blockers) can be used as an adjunct to benzodiazepines in select patients for control of persistent hypertension or tachycardia
    explanation: ASAM supports adjunct beta-blockers for persistent hypertension or tachycardia after benzodiazepines; this symptom control does not treat the underlying withdrawal process.
  target_mechanisms:
  - target: Withdrawal-Associated Autonomic Activation
    treatment_effect: INHIBITS
    description: Adjunctive symptom control does not correct the entire withdrawal process or protect against its severe neurologic complications.
    evidence:
    - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
      reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: OTHER
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      snippet: Alpha2-adrenergic agonists (AA2 s) such as clonidine and dexmedetomidine can be used as an adjunct to benzodiazepine therapy to control autonomic hyperactivity and anxiety when these signs are not controlled by benzodiazepines alone. They should not be used alone to prevent or treat withdrawal-related seizures or delirium.
      explanation: ASAM recommends alpha-2 agonists for adjunctive control of autonomic hyperactivity and anxiety, while explicitly excluding their use alone for seizures or delirium.
    - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
      reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: OTHER
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      snippet: Beta-adrenergic antagonists (beta-blockers) can be used as an adjunct to benzodiazepines in select patients for control of persistent hypertension or tachycardia
      explanation: ASAM supports adjunct beta-blockers for persistent hypertension or tachycardia after benzodiazepines; this symptom control does not treat the underlying withdrawal process.
biochemical:
- name: Phosphatidylethanol (PEth)
  presence: Elevated with recent heavy alcohol consumption
  specificity: Alcohol-exposure biomarker; diagnostic performance varies by threshold, exposure definition and population
  notes: A blood phospholipid formed in the presence of ethanol can support assessment of recent exposure over a period of weeks. The review included 12 heterogeneous studies of unhealthy drinking, not a uniform DSM AUD diagnostic cohort. Formation and elimination vary; concentrations do not uniquely recover a person’s daily intake or establish AUD. Reported study cutoffs ranged from 4.2 to 250 ng/mL.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:37569551
    reference_title: 'Phosphatidylethanol (PEth) in Blood as a Marker of Unhealthy Alcohol Use: A Systematic Review with Novel Molecular Insights.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: In recent years, phosphatidylethanol (PEth) in blood has emerged as a marker of unhealthy alcohol use.
    explanation: Systematic review establishes PEth as a biomarker of unhealthy alcohol use.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
  - reference: PMID:37569551
    reference_title: 'Phosphatidylethanol (PEth) in Blood as a Marker of Unhealthy Alcohol Use: A Systematic Review with Novel Molecular Insights.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: PEth interpretative cut-offs varied greatly among the included records, ranging from 4.2 ng/mL to 250 ng/mL, with sensitivity and specificity in the ranges of 58-100% and 64-100%, respectively.
    explanation: Quantifies the wide variation in reported cut-offs and diagnostic accuracy, which limits how prescriptively the marker can be used.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
- name: Gamma-Glutamyltransferase (GGT)
  presence: Elevated with sustained heavy alcohol consumption
  specificity: Low-moderate; individually insensitive and also elevated by non-alcoholic liver disease, obesity, and enzyme-inducing drugs
  notes: Indirect and nonspecific exposure-associated liver marker. In a selected study of 165 heavy drinkers versus moderate-drinker/abstainer references, sensitivity was 58% for GGT and 90% for the combined GGT-CDT index. In a different 1022-men/583-women study, GGT sensitivities were 30% and 23%; these are study-specific performance estimates, not universal accuracy. It does not diagnose AUD.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:16799164
    reference_title: Comparison of the combined marker GGT-CDT and the conventional laboratory markers of alcohol abuse in heavy drinkers, moderate drinkers and abstainers.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: The sensitivity of GGT-CDT (90%) in correctly classifying heavy drinkers exceeded that of CDT (63%), GGT (58%), mean corpuscular volume (MCV) (45%), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) (47%), and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) (50%), being also essentially similar for alcoholics with (93%) or without (88%) liver disease.
    explanation: Quantifies the sensitivity of each conventional marker and of the combined GGT-CDT index in a cohort of 165 heavy drinkers against moderate-drinker and abstainer references.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
  - reference: PMID:16799164
    reference_title: Comparison of the combined marker GGT-CDT and the conventional laboratory markers of alcohol abuse in heavy drinkers, moderate drinkers and abstainers.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: GGT-CDT improves the sensitivity of detecting excessive ethanol consumption as compared with the traditional markers of ethanol consumption.
    explanation: States the study's conclusion that the combined GGT-CDT index outperforms the individual conventional markers.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
  - reference: PMID:17767129
    reference_title: The Early Detection of Alcohol Consumption (EDAC) test shows better performance than gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) to detect heavy drinking in a large population of males and females.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: The results showed that 30% of males reporting heavy drinking tested GGT positive compared to 65% who tested EDAC positive.
    explanation: The male heavy-drinking subgroup had low GGT positivity at the study threshold, demonstrating that a normal result cannot exclude substantial consumption.
  - reference: PMID:17767129
    reference_title: The Early Detection of Alcohol Consumption (EDAC) test shows better performance than gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) to detect heavy drinking in a large population of males and females.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: For females, the results showed that 23% of those reporting heavy drinking tested GGT positive compared to 34% who tested EDAC positive.
    explanation: The female heavy-drinking subgroup also had limited GGT positivity, reinforcing the threshold- and population-specific nature of this marker.
  - reference: PMID:36983134
    reference_title: 'Old and New Biomarkers of Alcohol Abuse: Narrative Review.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: "[In the GGT row:] The specificity is reduced by obesity, diabetes, non-alcoholic liver diseases, pancreatitis, hyperlipidemia, heart failure, massive injuries, drugs (barbiturates, antiepileptic drugs, anticoagulants), kidney diseases."
    explanation: The GGT row of the review table names non-alcoholic causes of elevation, supporting limited specificity independently of the sensitivity cohorts.
  reference_ranges:
  - loinc_term:
      id: LOINC:2324-2
      label: Gamma glutamyl transferase [Enzymatic activity/volume] in Serum or Plasma
    upper_bound: 85.0
    unit: U/L
    population: males; screening cutoff for heavy drinking
    notes: Study-specific assay decision threshold for classifying alcohol exposure, not a universal clinical reference interval or diagnostic cutoff for AUD.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:17767129
      reference_title: The Early Detection of Alcohol Consumption (EDAC) test shows better performance than gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) to detect heavy drinking in a large population of males and females.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: The GGT test used a cutoff of 85 U/L for males and 65 U/L for females.
      explanation: Source of the sex-specific GGT cutoffs used to screen for heavy drinking.
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
  - loinc_term:
      id: LOINC:2324-2
      label: Gamma glutamyl transferase [Enzymatic activity/volume] in Serum or Plasma
    upper_bound: 65.0
    unit: U/L
    population: females; screening cutoff for heavy drinking
    notes: Study-specific assay decision threshold for classifying alcohol exposure, not a universal clinical reference interval or diagnostic cutoff for AUD.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:17767129
      reference_title: The Early Detection of Alcohol Consumption (EDAC) test shows better performance than gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) to detect heavy drinking in a large population of males and females.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: The GGT test used a cutoff of 85 U/L for males and 65 U/L for females.
      explanation: Source of the sex-specific GGT cutoffs used to screen for heavy drinking.
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
- name: Carbohydrate-Deficient Transferrin (CDT)
  presence: Elevated with sustained heavy alcohol consumption
  specificity: Moderate-high; the most specific of the conventional indirect markers, though affected by pregnancy, severe liver disease, and rare transferrin variants
  notes: Indirect marker of sustained alcohol exposure, not a diagnostic test for AUD. The 63% sensitivity and 90% combined GGT-CDT sensitivity came from the selected 165-heavy-drinker study. A separate forensic cohort of 562 people assessed percentage disialotransferrin with a 1.7% HPLC decision cutoff against hair EtG; neither the cutoff nor agreement proves complete abstinence.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:16799164
    reference_title: Comparison of the combined marker GGT-CDT and the conventional laboratory markers of alcohol abuse in heavy drinkers, moderate drinkers and abstainers.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: The sensitivity of GGT-CDT (90%) in correctly classifying heavy drinkers exceeded that of CDT (63%), GGT (58%), mean corpuscular volume (MCV) (45%), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) (47%), and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) (50%), being also essentially similar for alcoholics with (93%) or without (88%) liver disease.
    explanation: The heavy-drinker cohort supplies the CDT sensitivity and combined GGT-CDT estimate, separate from the HPLC decision threshold below.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
  - reference: PMID:36983134
    reference_title: 'Old and New Biomarkers of Alcohol Abuse: Narrative Review.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: '[In the CDT row:] The most specific marker available today. The specificity is reduced by rare genetic defects in transferrin. ... Certain diseases reduce the specificity of the CDT test. These include non-alcoholic liver diseases (primary biliary cirrhosis, chronic active inflammation, -HCV, hepatocellular carcinoma), senile dementia, depression, pregnancy'
    explanation: The review describes relatively high CDT specificity among conventional markers, while identifying rare transferrin variants and several non-alcoholic conditions that reduce it.
  reference_ranges:
  - loinc_term:
      id: LOINC:48495-6
      label: Transferrin.carbohydrate deficient/Transferrin.total in Serum or Plasma
    upper_bound: 1.7
    unit: '%'
    population: adults; %disialotransferrin by HPLC candidate reference method
    notes: Study-specific assay decision threshold for classifying alcohol exposure, not a universal clinical reference interval or diagnostic cutoff for AUD.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:25698630
      reference_title: A comparison between serum carbohydrate-deficient transferrin and hair ethyl glucuronide in detecting chronic alcohol consumption in routine.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: 'Serum CDT was measured by the candidate HPLC reference method and expressed as relative amount of disialotransferrin (%DST: cutoff 1.7%).'
      explanation: Source of the % CDT (disialotransferrin) upper-limit cutoff used clinically.
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
- name: Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)
  presence: Elevated with sustained heavy alcohol consumption (macrocytosis)
  specificity: Low; also elevated by folate/B12 deficiency, liver disease, hypothyroidism, and reticulocytosis independent of alcohol
  notes: Macrocytosis is nonspecific and can accompany sustained alcohol exposure or nutritional and other disease. The 45% sensitivity belongs to a selected 165-heavy-drinker study. The 96/98 fL upper limits came from 845 reference individuals classified as abstainers/moderate drinkers, not validated AUD diagnostic cutoffs.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:16799164
    reference_title: Comparison of the combined marker GGT-CDT and the conventional laboratory markers of alcohol abuse in heavy drinkers, moderate drinkers and abstainers.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: The sensitivity of GGT-CDT (90%) in correctly classifying heavy drinkers exceeded that of CDT (63%), GGT (58%), mean corpuscular volume (MCV) (45%), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) (47%), and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) (50%), being also essentially similar for alcoholics with (93%) or without (88%) liver disease.
    explanation: Quantifies MCV's individual sensitivity (45%) for classifying heavy drinkers, well below the combined GGT-CDT index.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
  - reference: PMID:36983134
    reference_title: 'Old and New Biomarkers of Alcohol Abuse: Narrative Review.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: The possible false positive increases in MCV include vitamin B12 and folic acid deficiency, hypothyroidism, hemolytic disease with reticulocytosis, non-alcoholic liver disease
    explanation: The review identifies alternative causes of macrocytosis; the heavy-drinker sensitivity estimate alone does not establish this specificity caveat.
  reference_ranges:
  - loinc_term:
      id: LOINC:30428-7
      label: MCV [Entitic mean volume] in Red Blood Cells
    upper_bound: 96.0
    unit: fL
    population: abstainers (NORIP reference data)
    notes: The LOINC code was verified against the NLM clinical-tables LOINC service; LOINC is not covered by the repository's OAK term validation.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:16581347
      reference_title: 'Long-term ethanol consumption and macrocytosis: diagnostic and pathogenic implications.'
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: the upper normal limit for MCV based on the data from moderate drinkers was 98 fl, as compared with 96 fl from abstainers
      explanation: Source of the abstainer upper normal limit for MCV, derived from NORIP reference data.
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
  - loinc_term:
      id: LOINC:30428-7
      label: MCV [Entitic mean volume] in Red Blood Cells
    upper_bound: 98.0
    unit: fL
    population: moderate drinkers (NORIP reference data)
    notes: The higher upper limit in moderate drinkers versus abstainers itself reflects a dose-related response of MCV to ethanol intake. The LOINC code was verified against the NLM clinical-tables LOINC service; LOINC is not covered by the repository's OAK term validation.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:16581347
      reference_title: 'Long-term ethanol consumption and macrocytosis: diagnostic and pathogenic implications.'
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: the upper normal limit for MCV based on the data from moderate drinkers was 98 fl, as compared with 96 fl from abstainers
      explanation: Source of the moderate-drinker upper normal limit for MCV, derived from NORIP reference data.
      directness: DIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
diagnosis:
- name: DSM-5-TR clinical diagnosis
  description: A problematic pattern causing clinically significant impairment or distress with any two or more of eleven criteria within a year supports diagnosis. Two or three criteria indicate mild, four or five moderate, and six or more severe AUD. Tolerance and withdrawal are optional criteria. Review history, functional impact, other substance use and psychiatric or medical explanations; exposure biomarkers alone do not diagnose AUD.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:37844924
    reference_title: Canadian guideline for the clinical management of high-risk drinking and alcohol use disorder.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: The diagnosis of AUD can be made when a patient has a problematic pattern of alcohol use over a year that leads to clinically significant impairment or distress, involving at least 2 of the 11 DSM-5-TR criteria.
    explanation: The guideline states the DSM-5-TR clinical threshold, supporting the diagnostic construct rather than a molecular cause of addiction.
  - reference: PMID:37844924
    reference_title: Canadian guideline for the clinical management of high-risk drinking and alcohol use disorder.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: Patients are diagnosed with mild AUD if they have 2–3 criteria; moderate AUD with 4–5 criteria; and severe AUD with 6 or more criteria.
    explanation: The DSM-5-TR severity bands count diagnostic criteria, rather than biological subtypes or withdrawal severity.
- name: ICD-11 alcohol diagnoses
  description: ICD-11 distinguishes alcohol dependence and harmful pattern of use; hazardous use is a separately listed health-risk factor. These categories should not be treated as exact synonyms for the DSM-5-TR severity spectrum.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:31194891
    reference_title: 'Alcohol Use Disorders in ICD-11: Past, Present, and Future.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: This review describes and discusses the alcohol diagnoses within this section of ICD-11, including Alcohol Dependence, Harmful Pattern of Use of Alcohol, and entities such as Alcohol Intoxication, Alcohol Withdrawal, and several alcohol-induced mental disorders, and briefly covers Hazardous Alcohol Use, which is listed separately as a health risk factor.
    explanation: Authoritative description of the ICD-11 alcohol diagnostic structure.
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
- name: AUDIT, AUDIT-C and brief screening
  description: Validated questionnaires identify unhealthy or high-risk drinking and prompt a diagnostic interview. Thresholds depend on the population and screening purpose. AUDIT-C assesses consumption, whereas the AUDIT problems subscale used in PAU genetics is a different measure. Neither is a stand-alone molecular or clinical confirmation of AUD.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:37844924
    reference_title: Canadian guideline for the clinical management of high-risk drinking and alcohol use disorder.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: The AUDIT and AUDIT-C tools were designed to screen for hazardous or harmful alcohol use, using a cut-off score of 8 (for AUDIT) or 3 and 4 for women and men, respectively (for AUDIT-C).
    explanation: The guideline provides screening thresholds for hazardous or harmful use, which require clinical follow-up rather than automatic AUD diagnosis.
  - reference: PMID:37844924
    reference_title: Canadian guideline for the clinical management of high-risk drinking and alcohol use disorder.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: Adults and youth who screen positive for high-risk drinking should undergo a diagnostic interview for mild, moderate or severe AUD using the DSM-5-TR criteria
    explanation: A positive screen prompts a diagnostic interview, explicitly separating screening from diagnosis.
- name: Withdrawal risk and severity assessment
  description: History of seizures or delirium, current findings, coexisting disease and available support guide the level of care. PAWSS predicts risk in studied medically ill populations; CIWA-Ar measures current withdrawal symptoms and can be confounded by other illness. CIWA-Ar depends on patient report and should not be used to assess delirium.
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: Most withdrawal severity scales reflect current signs and symptoms and should not be used alone to determine level of care.
    explanation: A current symptom score is not a complete risk or placement assessment, supporting the additional clinical factors described here.
  - reference: url:https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    reference_title: https://www.asam.org/docs/default-source/quality-science/the_asam_clinical_practice_guideline_on_alcohol-1.pdf
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    snippet: It is not recommended to use the CIWA-Ar in patients with delirium because it relies on patient-reported symptoms.
    explanation: The guideline excludes CIWA-Ar in delirium because reliable patient-reported symptoms are required.
clinical_trials:
- name: clinicaltrials:NCT05520775
  phase: PHASE_II
  status: COMPLETED
  description: Completed phase 2 trial randomized 48 nontreatment-seeking adults 21–65 with AUD and BMI≥23. Semaglutide 0.25 mg/week for 4 weeks then 0.5 mg/week for 4 weeks preceded the primary laboratory assessment; week 9 dose escalation followed primary collection. Paired laboratory analyses included 25 participants, so this was not a complete-case 48-person primary outcome. Registered calendar-day drinking was null; other weekly quantity/craving outcomes were exploratory.
  target_phenotypes:
  - preferred_term: Addictive alcohol use
    term:
      id: HP:0030955
      label: Addictive alcohol use
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:39937469
    reference_title: 'Once-Weekly Semaglutide in Adults With Alcohol Use Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Low-dose semaglutide reduced the amount of alcohol consumed during a posttreatment laboratory self-administration task, with evidence of medium to large effect sizes for grams of alcohol consumed
    explanation: Reports the primary laboratory self-administration outcome of this trial.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
  - reference: clinicaltrials:NCT05520775
    reference_title: Human Laboratory Screening of Semaglutide for Alcohol Use Disorder
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: This is an early-Phase II human laboratory trial using a randomized, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging design to investigate the effects of semaglutide, a GLP-1 receptor agonist, on alcohol-related outcomes in adults with alcohol use disorder (AUD).
    explanation: The registry summary describes study design; current status was separately checked through the live registry API and efficacy comes from the published report.
  notes: 'Live ClinicalTrials.gov API status checked 2026-09-21: COMPLETED, phase 2. Registry brief-summary caches support study identity; live API supplies current administrative status.'
- name: clinicaltrials:NCT05895643
  phase: PHASE_II
  status: COMPLETED
  description: Completed single-center 26-week phase 2 trial randomized 108 treatment-seeking adults with moderate/severe AUD and obesity (54 per group) to weekly semaglutide up to 2.4 mg or placebo, both with CBT. 88 completed; intention-to-treat primary analysis used multiple imputation. Adjusted heavy-drinking-day difference was −13.7 percentage points, not a relative 70% treatment benefit; long-term/general-population effects remain uncertain.
  target_phenotypes:
  - preferred_term: Problematic alcohol consumption
    term:
      id: HP:5200329
      label: Problematic alcohol consumption
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:42070571
    reference_title: 'Once-weekly semaglutide versus placebo in patients with alcohol use disorder and comorbid obesity: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: Semaglutide showed robust therapeutic effects in treatment-seeking participants with obesity and alcohol use disorder and this trial supports previous preclinical and clinical findings suggesting GLP-1 receptor agonists as a potential novel treatment target for alcohol use disorder.
    explanation: States the trial's overall conclusion for its treatment-seeking, comorbid-obesity population.
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
  - reference: clinicaltrials:NCT05895643
    reference_title: Does the Glucagon-like Peptide 1 (GLP-1) Receptor Agonist Semaglutide Reduce Alcohol Intake in Patients With Alcohol Use Disorder and Comorbid Obesity?
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: The medication will be provided as a supplement to standardised cognitive behavioural therapy.
    explanation: The registry summary describes study design; current status was separately checked through the live registry API and efficacy comes from the published report.
  notes: 'Live ClinicalTrials.gov API status checked 2026-09-21: COMPLETED, phase 2. Registry brief-summary caches support study identity; live API supplies current administrative status.'
animal_models:
- name: Alcohol-preferring P rats
  species: Rattus norvegicus
  genotype: Selectively bred P line
  description: Review of selected rats with voluntary ethanol intake, reinforcement and protocol-dependent binge/deprivation responses. The historical animal criteria are not DSM-5-TR criteria, and neither human age at onset nor all AUD domains are reproduced. Intoxicating concentrations depend on the access paradigm.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:24268381
    reference_title: The alcohol-preferring (P) and high-alcohol-drinking (HAD) rats--animal models of alcoholism.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: The P line of rats meets all of the originally proposed criteria for a suitable animal model of alcoholism.
    explanation: The review characterizes the selectively bred P rat as an experimental alcoholism model; model criteria are not equivalent to a human diagnosis.
  - reference: PMID:24268381
    reference_title: The alcohol-preferring (P) and high-alcohol-drinking (HAD) rats--animal models of alcoholism.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: The P line also exhibits excessive binge-like alcohol drinking, attaining blood alcohol concentrations (BACs) of 200 mg% on a daily basis.
    explanation: Reported high blood alcohol levels support the line's binge-like exposure phenotype under the reviewed experimental conditions.
  modeled_mechanisms:
  - target: Repeated Ethanol Exposure
    relationship: MEASURES
    fidelity: MODERATE
    description: Voluntary intake and binge-access endpoints model high alcohol exposure.
    limitations: Selection for intake is not a model of every clinical criterion or an established human causal allele.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:24268381
      reference_title: The alcohol-preferring (P) and high-alcohol-drinking (HAD) rats--animal models of alcoholism.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
      directness: DIRECT
      snippet: Under 24-h free-choice conditions, the P rat will voluntarily consume 5–8 g/kg/day and produce BACs in the range of 50–200 mg%
      explanation: The review reports voluntary ethanol intake and attained blood alcohol concentrations under a specified free-choice protocol.
    readouts:
    - name: Voluntary ethanol intake
      target: Repeated Ethanol Exposure
      direction: INCREASED
      interpretation: Voluntary intake and binge-access endpoints model high alcohol exposure.
      evidence:
      - reference: PMID:24268381
        reference_title: The alcohol-preferring (P) and high-alcohol-drinking (HAD) rats--animal models of alcoholism.
        supports: SUPPORT
        evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
        quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
        directness: DIRECT
        snippet: Under 24-h free-choice conditions, the P rat will voluntarily consume 5–8 g/kg/day and produce BACs in the range of 50–200 mg%
        explanation: The review reports voluntary ethanol intake and attained blood alcohol concentrations under a specified free-choice protocol.
- name: High-alcohol-drinking HAD rat lines
  species: Rattus norvegicus
  genotype: Selectively bred HAD1 and HAD2 lines
  description: The reviewed HAD lines show high intake and deprivation-related responses under specific protocols. The review reports four of six historical animal criteria, with tolerance and withdrawal not examined; the P-line completeness statement must not be transferred to HAD.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:24268381
    reference_title: The alcohol-preferring (P) and high-alcohol-drinking (HAD) rats--animal models of alcoholism.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: The HAD1,2 rats satisfy several of the criteria for an animal model of alcoholism, e.g., these rats will voluntarily consume ethanol in a free-choice situation to produce BACs between 50 and 200 mg%.
    explanation: Voluntary drinking in HAD lines produces substantial blood alcohol concentrations, supporting an exposure model without implying all human AUD features.
  modeled_mechanisms:

    relationship: MEASURES
    fidelity: MODERATE
    description: Selected high-drinking lines model voluntary exposure.
    limitations: Unexamined tolerance and withdrawal domains limit correspondence to physiological dependence.

      explanation: Voluntary drinking in HAD lines produces substantial blood alcohol concentrations, supporting an exposure model without implying all human AUD features.

- name: HAP/LAP preference QTL mouse cross
  species: Mus musculus
  genotype: High Alcohol Preferring (HAP1, HAP2) and Low Alcohol Preferring (LAP1, LAP2) lines
  description: The 2006 study used a 432-animal F2 cross derived from selectively bred, outbred high- and low-preference lines. A chromosome 9 QTL had stronger support in females. Historical wording about the only extant lines is not a current inventory claim, and mouse preference mapping does not identify a human causal AUD gene.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:16482403
    reference_title: Identification of QTLs influencing alcohol preference in the High Alcohol Preferring (HAP) and Low Alcohol Preferring (LAP) mouse lines.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: The High- and Low-Alcohol Preferring (HAP1/LAP1 and HAP2/LAP2) mouse lines were developed by selective breeding for differences in alcohol preference.
    explanation: Selective breeding establishes genetically divergent preference lines for QTL analysis, rather than a single-gene model of human addiction.
  modeled_mechanisms:
  - target: Repeated Ethanol Exposure
    relationship: MEASURES
    fidelity: MODERATE
    description: Alcohol preference varied in a segregating HAP1 × LAP1 F2 cross and was linked to a chromosome 9 QTL; no single increase relative to a control is asserted.
    limitations: Preference is not equivalent to clinical compulsivity, withdrawal or DSM diagnosis.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:16482403
      reference_title: Identification of QTLs influencing alcohol preference in the High Alcohol Preferring (HAP) and Low Alcohol Preferring (LAP) mouse lines.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      directness: DIRECT
      snippet: In Study 2, a genome-wide screen was performed in a sample of 432 HAP1xLAP1 F2 animals and a QTL on chromosome 9 (LOD=5.04) was found which met criteria for genome wide significance (p<0.001). ... This study provides additional evidence and confirmation that specific regions on chromosomes 9 and perhaps 2 are important for alcohol preference.
      explanation: The study maps alcohol-preference variation in the F2 cross; it does not report a uniformly increased phenotype in that cross.
    readouts:
    - name: Alcohol preference
      target: Repeated Ethanol Exposure
      interpretation: Alcohol preference varied in a segregating HAP1 × LAP1 F2 cross and was linked to a chromosome 9 QTL; no single increase relative to a control is asserted.
      evidence:
      - reference: PMID:16482403
        reference_title: Identification of QTLs influencing alcohol preference in the High Alcohol Preferring (HAP) and Low Alcohol Preferring (LAP) mouse lines.
        supports: SUPPORT
        evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
        quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
        directness: DIRECT
        snippet: In Study 2, a genome-wide screen was performed in a sample of 432 HAP1xLAP1 F2 animals and a QTL on chromosome 9 (LOD=5.04) was found which met criteria for genome wide significance (p<0.001). ... This study provides additional evidence and confirmation that specific regions on chromosomes 9 and perhaps 2 are important for alcohol preference.
        explanation: The study maps alcohol-preference variation in the F2 cross; it does not report a uniformly increased phenotype in that cross.
- name: HDID selected-line aversion and reward assays
  species: Mus musculus
  genotype: High Drinking in the Dark (HDID-1, HDID-2) selected lines, from an HS/Npt heterogeneous stock
  description: Two selected replicates were compared with concurrent heterogeneous-stock controls. Conditioned taste aversion was attenuated at a moderate 2 g/kg ethanol dose but not at 4 g/kg; details varied by replicate and analysis. Conditioned place preference at the tested 2 g/kg dose did not differ. This genetic co-occurrence does not prove reduced aversion mediates every animal’s intake or absence of all reward differences.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:23910826
    reference_title: Rewarding and aversive effects of ethanol in High Drinking in the Dark selectively bred mice.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: These results indicate that high blood alcohol levels after drinking in the HDID mice is genetically related to attenuated aversion to alcohol, while sensitivity to alcohol reward is not altered in these mice.
    explanation: Selected HDID mice show reduced conditioned aversion without increased reward sensitivity, separating those candidate contributors to high blood alcohol levels.
  - reference: PMID:23910826
    reference_title: Rewarding and aversive effects of ethanol in High Drinking in the Dark selectively bred mice.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: HDID and HS mice showed comparable development of alcohol-induced conditioned place preference.
    explanation: Comparable conditioned place preference constrains the interpretation that HDID selection simply increased alcohol reward.
  modeled_mechanisms:
  - target: Repeated Ethanol Exposure
    relationship: MEASURES
    fidelity: MODERATE
    description: Blood ethanol concentrations after a four-hour drinking-in-the-dark test increased in both selected replicate lines relative to the founding generation; aversion and reward were assessed in separate experiments.
    limitations: Separate animals and dose-specific conditioning endpoints do not resolve a universal reward mechanism.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:24219304
      reference_title: Progress in a replicated selection for elevated blood ethanol concentrations in HDID mice.
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      directness: DIRECT
      snippet: High Drinking in the Dark (HDID-1) mice have been bred for 27 selected generations (S27) for elevated blood ethanol concentrations (BECs) after a 4-h period of access to 20% ethanol. A second replicate line (HDID-2) was started later from the same founder population and is currently in S20. ... the lines have shown 4-5 fold increases in BEC since S0
      explanation: Both HDID replicate lines showed increased blood ethanol concentrations across selection generations; this is a drinking measurement, separate from the conditioning assays.
    readouts:
    - name: Blood alcohol after limited-access drinking
      target: Repeated Ethanol Exposure
      direction: INCREASED
      interpretation: Blood ethanol concentrations after a four-hour drinking-in-the-dark test increased in both selected replicate lines relative to the founding generation; aversion and reward were assessed in separate experiments.
      evidence:
      - reference: PMID:24219304
        reference_title: Progress in a replicated selection for elevated blood ethanol concentrations in HDID mice.
        supports: SUPPORT
        evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
        quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
        directness: DIRECT
        snippet: High Drinking in the Dark (HDID-1) mice have been bred for 27 selected generations (S27) for elevated blood ethanol concentrations (BECs) after a 4-h period of access to 20% ethanol. A second replicate line (HDID-2) was started later from the same founder population and is currently in S20. ... the lines have shown 4-5 fold increases in BEC since S0
        explanation: Both HDID replicate lines showed increased blood ethanol concentrations across selection generations; this is a drinking measurement, separate from the conditioning assays.
- name: P-rat seeking-taking and outcome-devaluation paradigm
  species: Rattus norvegicus
  genotype: Male alcohol-preferring rats
  description: After intermittent two-bottle pre-exposure and seeking-taking training, devaluation-resistant seeking predicted punishment resistance and quinine-adulterated drinking. Similar earlier preference/intake did not account for all later differences. Available evidence here is the abstract; the study does not directly demonstrate a dorsal-striatal dopamine measurement in its reported experiments.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:33955649
    reference_title: Individual differences in the engagement of habitual control over alcohol seeking predict the development of compulsive alcohol seeking and drinking.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: After seeking behaviour was well established, subjects that had developed greater resistance to outcome devaluation (were more habitual) were more likely to show punishment-resistant (compulsive) alcohol seeking.
    explanation: Outcome-devaluation resistance predicted punishment-resistant seeking in selected rats; the association does not prove that habitual control alone causes human compulsive drinking.

- name: Chronic intermittent ethanol rodent paradigms
  species: Rattus norvegicus
  genotype: Repeated high-dose intermittent ethanol and withdrawal
  description: The review synthesizes hippocampal receptor redistribution and endpoint-dependent behavioral adaptation. Persistence was measured for 40–120 days in cited rat protocols; the quotation’s lifelong extension is speculation. Sedative and tonic-current tolerance does not imply tolerance to every anxiolytic or anticonvulsant effect. PTZ susceptibility is not a demonstrated spontaneous withdrawal seizure phenotype.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:28931433
    reference_title: Role of GABA(A) receptors in alcohol use disorders suggested by chronic intermittent ethanol (CIE) rodent model.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: After chronic intermittent ethanol (CIE) treatment the same changes are observed but they become persistent after 30 or more doses, lasting for at least 120 days in the rat, and probably for life.
    explanation: The reviewed rat regimen documents persistence for at least 120 days; the source's additional lifetime speculation is not treated as an observed endpoint.
  modeled_mechanisms:
  - target: GABA-A Receptor Redistribution
    relationship: MEASURES
    fidelity: MODERATE
    description: Repeated exposure changes receptor composition and localization over measured follow-up.
    limitations: Region-, compartment- and time-specific rodent changes are not a validated irreversible human threshold.

- name: Regional CRF pharmacology in DID and intermittent-access mice
  species: Mus musculus
  genotype: Male C57BL/6J mice; separate nondependent DID and four-week IAA cohorts
  description: VTA CRF6–33 and astressin 2-B reduced DID intake under selected doses; co-infusion supported additive modulation. CRF6–33 had no significant VTA effect in IAA and no CeA effect in either paradigm. Only IAA increased withdrawal handling-induced convulsions. Water intake and weight were assessed, but comprehensive locomotor or alternative-reward specificity was not established.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:26247973
    reference_title: 'Corticotropin Releasing Factor Binding Protein and CRF2 Receptors in the Ventral Tegmental Area: Modulation of Ethanol Binge Drinking in C57BL/6J Mice.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: These results indicate that VTA CRF2 receptors modulate ethanol binge drinking, and CRFBP may add to the anti-alcohol effect of A2B.
    explanation: Local VTA pharmacology modifies drinking in the nondependent binge paradigm; the result does not establish the same effect in dependence or in all brain regions.
  - reference: PMID:26247973
    reference_title: 'Corticotropin Releasing Factor Binding Protein and CRF2 Receptors in the Ventral Tegmental Area: Modulation of Ethanol Binge Drinking in C57BL/6J Mice.'
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Intra-CeA CRF6–33 neither affected ethanol binge drinking nor escalated ethanol consumption in mice given IAA.
    explanation: The central-amygdala null result limits regional generalization of the VTA CRF-binding-protein finding.
  modeled_mechanisms:
  - target: VTA CRF2-Associated Drinking Modulation
    relationship: MEASURES
    fidelity: MODERATE
    description: VTA antagonism reduces intake in the tested DID context.
    limitations: Does not establish dependent negative-reinforcement signaling, central-amygdala benefit, a dopamine intermediary or clinical efficacy.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:26247973
      reference_title: 'Corticotropin Releasing Factor Binding Protein and CRF2 Receptors in the Ventral Tegmental Area: Modulation of Ethanol Binge Drinking in C57BL/6J Mice.'
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      directness: DIRECT
      snippet: Here, we present the first evidence that the CRFBP antagonist CRF6–33 and the CRF2 antagonist A2B microinjected into the VTA dose-dependently attenuated alcohol consumption in mice exposed to a binge drinking procedure (DID).
      explanation: Intra-VTA CRF2 antagonism reduced intake in the DID experiment; the separate CeA null result supports the regional limitation only.

- name: Chronic ethanol exposure in constitutive Tlr4-knockout mice
  species: Mus musculus
  genotype: Female C57BL/6 wild-type versus constitutive Tlr4-knockout
  description: Starting at 7 weeks, mice received 10% ethanol in drinking water for 5 months; reported intake and blood alcohol concentrations were similar between genotypes. Cortical inflammatory proteins/transcripts, glial immunoreactivity and cleaved caspase-3 were measured. Knockout attenuated outcomes, with residual GFAP response. Neither alcohol seeking, cognition nor neuron-specific death was directly tested.
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6634595/
    reference_title: Pivotal Role of TLR4 Receptors in Alcohol-Induced Neuroinflammation and Brain Damage - PMC
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Our findings support the critical role of the TLR4 response in the neuroinflammation, brain injury, and possibly in the neurodegeneration induced by chronic ethanol intake.
    explanation: The mouse study supports receptor dependence of measured inflammatory and injury markers; neurodegeneration was proposed rather than a measured clinical outcome.
  modeled_mechanisms:
  - target: Cortical Inflammatory Mediator Induction
    relationship: MEASURES
    fidelity: MODERATE
    description: Chronic ethanol increases the measured endpoint in wild-type mice, with attenuation in Tlr4-deficient mice.
    limitations: Whole-body deletion and whole-tissue measurements do not establish cell autonomy or a human AUD phenotype.
    evidence:
    - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6634595/
      reference_title: Pivotal Role of TLR4 Receptors in Alcohol-Induced Neuroinflammation and Brain Damage - PMC
      supports: SUPPORT
      evidence_source: MODEL_ORGANISM
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      directness: DIRECT
      snippet: chronic ethanol treatment upregulated the levels of TNF-α, IL-1β, and mRNA IL-6 in the cortex homogenates of the WT mice, whereas no changes were observed in the levels of these cytokines in the cerebral cortices of the TLR4-KO mice.
      explanation: The wild-type versus knockout comparison shows TLR4-dependent cortical cytokine changes in mice; homogenate measurements do not identify every producing cell.
    readouts:

      target: Cortical Inflammatory Mediator Induction

discussions:
- discussion_id: aud_model_translation
  kind: HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH
  prompt: Which experimental receptor and stress-system adaptations causally contribute to clinically defined AUD in humans?
  attaches_to:
  - pathophysiology#GABA-A Receptor Redistribution
  - pathophysiology#CRF-Associated Stress Signaling
  - pathophysiology#Dynorphin–Kappa-Opioid Signaling
  - pathophysiology#TLR4-Dependent Inflammatory Signaling
  rationale: Rodent exposure, preference and drinking-in-the-dark paradigms interrogate distinct endpoints. They do not reproduce every diagnostic feature, and region-, time- and genotype-dependent effects limit a universal mechanistic chain. Human imaging, genetic associations and treatment efficacy cannot by themselves prove mediation through these specific experimental processes.
- discussion_id: aud_habit_system_human_fidelity
  kind: HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH
  prompt: Does devaluation-insensitive alcohol seeking causally mediate persistent harmful drinking in humans?
  attaches_to:
  - pathophysiology#Habitual Alcohol Seeking
  rationale: The curated rat study relates behavioral habit measures to later punishment resistance. Its abstract does not itself measure the proposed dorsal-striatal dopamine mechanism, and the correspondence to human diagnostic loss of control requires direct testing.
- discussion_id: aud_heterogeneity_and_comorbidity
  kind: KNOWLEDGE_GAP
  prompt: Which clinical trajectories reflect exposure effects, pre-existing liability or bidirectional comorbidity?
  attaches_to:
  - phenotypes#Depression
  - pathophysiology#Impaired Executive Control
  - pathophysiology#Polygenic Liability
  rationale: Cross-sectional psychiatric associations and MRI differences do not isolate causal direction. The depression study selected people with major depressive disorder, not an unselected AUD population. Genetic PAU combines heterogeneous diagnoses and questionnaire measures; current polygenic scores are not sufficient for individual clinical risk prediction.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:38062264
    reference_title: Multi-ancestry study of the genetics of problematic alcohol use in over 1 million individuals.
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: We note that the current findings are not sufficient for clinical risk prediction at the individual level, given the limited SNP-based heritability and small proportion of variance explained by PRS.
    explanation: The authors explicitly reject individual clinical risk prediction from the current results, limiting use of the PAU polygenic score.

experimental_models:
- name: Neonatal rodent astrocyte TLR4 perturbations
  experimental_model_type: PRIMARY_CELL_CULTURE
  cell_source: Neonatal rat astrocytes with TLR4, CD14 or MD-2 siRNA; separate wild-type and Tlr4-knockout mouse astrocytes
  publication: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6634595/
  description: Highly enriched astrocyte cultures were exposed to ethanol with non-targeting siRNA and LPS-related controls. Rat knockdown experiments used 50 mM ethanol, whereas mouse knockout cultures used 10 mM. Nuclear p65, pERK and inflammatory readouts support TLR4 dependence. Lipopolysaccharide contamination controls were performed, but direct ethanol–TLR4 binding was not resolved.
  evidence:
  - reference: url:https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6634595/
    reference_title: Pivotal Role of TLR4 Receptors in Alcohol-Induced Neuroinflammation and Brain Damage - PMC
    supports: SUPPORT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    directness: DIRECT
    snippet: Gene silencing of TLR4 downregulates the TLR4 expression and reduces NFκB activation induced by ethanol in astrocytes in culture.
    explanation: TLR4 knockdown reduces ethanol-induced NF-kappa-B activation in cultured astrocytes, establishing a perturbation result within that cell preparation.
  modeled_mechanisms:
  - target: Astrocytic NF-kappa-B Activation
    relationship: MEASURES
    fidelity: MODERATE
    description: TLR4 knockdown attenuates ethanol-associated nuclear p65 signaling.
    limitations: Neonatal cell culture is distinct from intact adult human cortex and clinical addiction.

New Disease entry for Alcohol Use Disorder, bound to MONDO:0007079 (alcohol dependence) as the closest MONDO term to the DSM-5 construct; the terminology caveat is recorded in the entry's notes. Deep-research provider: claude_code. Run via `just research-disorder claude_code Alcohol_Use_Disorder`; 18 web searches over 16 turns, 34 citations, report at research/Alcohol_Use_Disorder-deep-research-claude_code.md. NEC preflight: `just preflight-dr research/Alcohol_Use_Disorder-deep-research-claude_code.md MONDO:0007079` returned SKIP, because MONDO records no causal gene for this complex trait and the automated gene check cannot discriminate. The manual fallback checks passed: the report's asserted OMIM 103780 matches the MONDO OMIM xref, the report's top gene mentions (ALDH2, ADH1B) are the correct alcohol-metabolism loci for this entity, and the queried name matches MONDO's synonym list (alcoholism / alcohol dependence). DR outputs were treated as leads, not ground truth, and every identifier was independently verified. Four errors were found and corrected: three HGNC IDs supplied by the report were wrong (hgnc:249 is ADH1A, not ADH1B; hgnc:4083 is GABRB3, not GABRA2; hgnc:24578 is DDI2, not KLB), replaced with OAK-verified hgnc:250, hgnc:4076, hgnc:15527; and the heritability PMID it supplied (25066582) is an unrelated orthopedics paper, replaced with the correct Verhulst/Neale/Kendler meta-analysis PMID:25171596. The report also proposed GO:0038003 as a molecular function and several HPO IDs that did not match their stated labels; these were corrected against OAK before use. Content curated. Pathograph: 14 pathophysiology nodes implementing the Koob-Volkow three-stage addiction cycle - polygenic and metabolic-gene susceptibility; ethanol oxidative metabolism; the protective acetaldehyde-flush branch; acute GABA-A potentiation and NMDA inhibition; mesolimbic dopamine and endogenous opioid reward; incentive salience and cue reactivity; GABAergic-glutamatergic neuroadaptation and tolerance; withdrawal hyperexcitability; extended-amygdala stress-system recruitment; hyperkatifeia and reward deficit; dorsolateral striatal habit recruitment; prefrontal executive control deficit; compulsive seeking and loss of control; sustained exposure and multiorgan toxicity. Also 21 phenotypes, 6 genetic entries (ADH1B and ALDH2 as PROTECTIVE, GABRA2/GCKR/KLB as SUSCEPTIBILITY, OPRM1 as a contested MODIFIER carrying a REFUTE evidence item from the genotype-stratified trial), 1 environmental exposure with influences_mechanisms edges, 10 treatments, 2 prevalence records, 1 biochemical marker, 2 diagnosis records, 2 clinical trials, and 2 discussions (KNOWLEDGE_GAP on translating extended-amygdala stress pharmacology to humans; HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH on the rodent-derived habit-system claim). Scope decision: end-organ sequelae of chronic drinking are deliberately shallow because Alcoholic_Liver_Disease is a separate entry. Those phenotypes carry supports: PARTIAL, with the missing organ-specific citation named in the explanation rather than papered over. Three known gaps are recorded in the entry's notes rather than left implicit: the neuroimmune/TLR4 arm is not modelled as its own node (no abstract-quotable primary source verified this session), the PARTIAL end-organ phenotypes need organ-specific references, and the indirect biomarkers GGT/CDT/MCV are not curated alongside PEth. A self-review pass against the dismech-pr-review content-completeness checklist added three things the first draft had missed: a Craving phenotype (DSM-5 criterion, deliberately left unbound because HPO has only food-specific craving terms - flagged as an NTR candidate), baclofen as an off-label treatment, and an incoming causal edge to the prefrontal executive-control node so it is no longer a graph root.
